# AI visibility for skin care clinics

> When someone asks ChatGPT for a skin care clinic in your town, we work to have you in the answer. Free AI Score, then the work that moves it.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/for/skin-care-clinics/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Skin care clinics

**Short answer** When someone asks ChatGPT for a skin care clinic near you, you're in the answer. We get you there by making your business easy for AI to confirm: consistent listings, an active Google profile, reviews with replies, and coverage on other sites.

Almost every question in this trade is about a condition rather than a clinic, and the businesses named in those answers are the ones whose pages describe the condition.

**The goal:** When someone asks ChatGPT for a skin care clinic near you, you're in the answer.

## What skin care clinics are up against

Dry skin, skin tags, anti-wrinkle treatment and red light therapy are the four topics the demand table holds most of. None of them is a business name.

That is an opportunity and a trap. A page that explains a procedure gets retrieved. A page that promises the procedure will work is an advertising problem.

New data from our research team

**76.4%**

Local business searches triggered a Google AI Overview 76.4% of the time, compared with 13.7% of all searches. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

**85.6%**

In a census of every venue in two markets, 85.6% were never recommended by any of four assistants. Being named was associated with having a website, more reviews, listed prices and web mentions (Pitenin 2026, preprint, reviewed in our brief). [How Often AI Recommends Your Business, LAIR-R-2026-002](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html)

## What people ask AI about skin care clinics

These are the questions people put to ChatGPT, Gemini and Google about skin care clinics, ranked by how often they're searched. None of them names a business. The assistant decides who to name.

| The question | Searches a year |
| --- | --- |
| What are the options for skin tag removal at a dermatologist? | 24,120 |
| What treatments are available for dry skin at a skin care clinic? | 10,860 |
| Do skin care clinics offer anti-wrinkle treatments? | 16,200 |
| What is the process for skin tag removal at a clinic? | 13,200 |
| Are there any skin care clinics offering red light therapy for skin rejuvenation? | 7,260 |

Questions are real rows from Local AI Registry's production demand data, as businesses in this industry asked them. The yearly figure is Google's ask volume for the keyword behind each question. Where a question named a town, the town was taken out.

## What we do for skin care clinics

The work that matters most here, and the feature page that explains each one in full.

### [Posts](../../signals/google-profile/index.html)

A post per topic, answering what the treatment is and what happens in the room, written from the services on your own record.

### [Photo work](../../signals/photo-codifying/index.html)

Pictures carrying the service name and the town in their own metadata, published a few at a time.

### [AI capture](../../signals/ai-monitoring/index.html)

Your questions asked every month, so you can watch a topic go from somebody else being named to you being named.

From our data · 3D

## What people ask AI about skin care clinics

Source: [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html), Local AI Registry research, 2026.

Two things follow. First, consistent listings are the floor, not the ceiling: almost no answer repeats your address or phone, so a listings tool alone can't put you in the answer. Second, the sources shift when a question is worded differently, so you need to watch many phrasings every month, not one keyword. In our own [AI Answer Watch](../../answer-watch/index.html) screenshots, 27 of 30 ChatGPT answers we screenshotted listed RealSelf among their sources, which is why industry review sites matter so much in medical aesthetics.

## The directories that matter for skin care clinics

Every business gets checked on 23 general directories: Yelp, Apple Maps, Facebook, the BBB, Yellow Pages, Foursquare, Nextdoor, Trustpilot and the rest. Because AI reads you as a beauty business, your roster grows to 29 with the beauty and wellness sites your customers use. A directory where we can't find you is recorded as not found, which is a different fact from not listed, and every reading is retired after 30 days so you never see a stale number.

## Your first 90 days

1. **Week 1: the baseline** We ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini the questions above, anchored to your town, and keep the screenshots. You see who is named today, and whether you are.
2. **Weeks 1 to 4: the record** You confirm your facts once. We fix your Google profile, audit your directories and order the missing ones.
3. **Every week: the work** Posts, review replies and photos go to your approval queue. Nothing goes live without your OK.
4. **Day 90: the check** If AI isn't naming you, we keep working free until it does.

## Frequently asked questions

Our treatments are on our website already. Why is that not enough?

Retrieval happens at passage level. A services page that lists names without describing them has nothing an answer can quote, which is a different problem from not existing.

Can you write about products we sell?

We can name a product you stock. We cannot say what it will do to somebody, which is where most product copy in this trade goes wrong.

# Why I built Local AI Registry.

> Why former Google and Microsoft executive Steve Lee left the corporate track, opened a med spa, and built Local AI Registry so local businesses can see what AI.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/founder-story/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Founder story

I spent 20 years inside the systems that decide what people find. Then I became the local business owner on the other side of them, and I didn’t like what I saw.

Chapter 1

## Building the systems

I built and sold my first company at 14. From there I spent two decades in digital: in Search at Google, at Microsoft on HoloLens, at Razorfish, Spotify, Chase and Kaplan. I was Head of Digital at Evolus through its 2018 Nasdaq IPO. I founded UX Laboratory, which was acquired. Along the way I’ve helped more than 5,000 local businesses get found.

## Choosing home

The corporate track meant living on planes. Around the time I was deciding what came next, my daughter needed open-heart surgery. That settled it. I stepped off the corporate track, stopped the constant travel and chose to stay local: close to my family, and close to the small businesses that make a community worth living in.

It’s why part of what we earn goes to the [Children’s Heart Foundation](../giving-back/index.html).

# Local AI search glossary

> Plain-language definitions of GEO, AEO, AI Overviews, entities, schema markup, llms.txt, AI Score and other local AI search terms.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/glossary/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Glossary

Plain definitions of the terms you'll meet when you work on getting your business recommended by AI. Each one says what the term means, why it matters for a local business and what to do about it.

## AEO (answer engine optimization)

**Writing and structuring content so assistants and search features can lift a direct answer from it.**

AEO puts the answer first: a clear two-sentence response to the question, followed by detail, an FAQ and [schema markup](../glossary/index.html#schema-markup). It overlaps with [GEO](../glossary/index.html#geo); AEO is about how your pages are written, GEO is about the wider set of sources AI trusts.

Related: [GEO (generative engine optimization)](../glossary#geo/index.html), [AI Overviews](../glossary#ai-overviews/index.html), [Schema markup](../glossary#schema-markup/index.html)

New data from our research team

**73%**

73% of the 128,400+ local businesses Local AI Registry has scored are named by zero AI assistants (our estimate from AI-visibility checks). [Local AI Registry data](../methodology/index.html)

## What does the research say?

From [The Local Answer Gap](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html), our study of how Google's AI answers local business questions. Every number links to its chart.

[**76.4%** of local business searches showed a Google AI answer, more than any other topic](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#google-ai-overview-activation-by-search-category)[**147 vs 70** times a store's own site ranked on page one, vs times the AI cited it, across 157 brand questions](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#brand-website-ranked-vs-cited-google-ai-overviews)

**SEO gets you into the list. AEO gets you into the answer.** Search engine optimization (SEO) earns a place in a list of links. Answer engine optimization (AEO) earns a place inside the AI-written answer that appears before any links.Illustration 1, [The Local Answer Gap](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../research/local-answer-gap/images/seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration.svg) · [PNG](../research/local-answer-gap/images/seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration.png)

**One confirmed record, pushed everywhere AI looks.** Because AI rotates between sources, a business’s facts need to match on its website, Google Business Profile, directories and press. Local AI Registry starts from one owner-confirmed record.Illustration 6, [The Local Answer Gap](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../research/local-answer-gap/images/single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration.svg) · [PNG](../research/local-answer-gap/images/single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration.png)

## AI Overviews

**The AI-written summaries Google shows above some search results.**

AI Overviews summarize an answer and link to sources. For local questions they draw on Google's search index and local business data. Google's AI Mode is a separate, conversational search built on the same data. See [how to show up in Google's AI answers](../ai/google-ai-overviews/index.html).

Related: [AEO (answer engine optimization)](../glossary#aeo/index.html), [Entity](../glossary#entity/index.html)

## AI Score

**Local AI Registry's measure of how ready a business is to be recommended by AI, based on the 11 signals.**

The AI Score looks at all [11 signals](../signals/index.html) AI uses to decide which local business to recommend and summarizes them in one number, with the detail behind it. Our [free AI visibility check](../tools/ai-visibility-check/index.html) starts with it.

Related: [AI visibility](../glossary#ai-visibility/index.html), [AI share of voice](../glossary#share-of-voice/index.html), [Local AI Blueprint™](../glossary#local-ai-blueprint/index.html)

## AI SEO

**A broad term for search optimization that accounts for AI answers as well as traditional rankings.**

People use AI SEO to mean anything from using AI tools to write content to optimizing for AI assistants. On this site we mean the second: making sure AI assistants recommend your business. See [GEO](../glossary/index.html#geo) and [AEO](../glossary/index.html#aeo).

Related: [GEO (generative engine optimization)](../glossary#geo/index.html), [AEO (answer engine optimization)](../glossary#aeo/index.html)

## AI share of voice

**The share of relevant AI answers that name your business compared with competitors.**

If you ask 20 customer questions across several assistants and you are named in 6 of the answers, that is your share of voice for that question set. Tracking it monthly is the core of [AI monitoring](../signals/ai-monitoring/index.html).

Related: [AI Score](../glossary#ai-score/index.html), [AI visibility](../glossary#ai-visibility/index.html)

## AI visibility

**How often, and how well, AI assistants mention and recommend a business when people ask questions it could answer.**

AI visibility is to assistants what search rankings are to Google. A business with strong AI visibility is named when someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Google's AI answers for the kind of service it offers, and it is described accurately. It depends on [eleven signals](../signals/index.html), from [consistent listings](../signals/directory-listings/index.html) to [reviews](../signals/reputation/index.html).

Related: [GEO (generative engine optimization)](../glossary#geo/index.html), [AEO (answer engine optimization)](../glossary#aeo/index.html), [AI Score](../glossary#ai-score/index.html)

## Citation

**A mention of your business on another website, or a source an AI assistant links to in its answer.**

The word has two uses. In local SEO, a citation is any listing or page that mentions your business details. In AI answers, a citation is a source the assistant shows to back up what it said. Being cited by AI usually starts with being cited around the web.

Related: [NAP consistency](../glossary#nap-consistency/index.html), [GEO (generative engine optimization)](../glossary#geo/index.html)

## Entity

**A distinct, identifiable thing, such as a business, person or place, that search engines and AI track as one object with known facts.**

To an assistant, your business is an entity with a name, location, category, services, people and reviews. The clearer and more consistent those facts are across the web, the more confidently AI can talk about you. [Schema markup](../glossary/index.html#schema-markup) and [NAP consistency](../glossary/index.html#nap-consistency) are how you make your entity clear.

Related: [Knowledge graph](../glossary#knowledge-graph/index.html), [NAP consistency](../glossary#nap-consistency/index.html), [Structured data](../glossary#structured-data/index.html)

## GEO (generative engine optimization)

**The practice of improving how a business or brand appears in answers written by AI assistants.**

GEO focuses on the sources AI reads and cites: reviews, articles, lists, structured data and your own pages. For a local business, GEO means making sure every assistant can confirm who you are, what you do and why you're a good choice. See how it compares with traditional SEO in [AI visibility vs SEO](../signals/seo/index.html).

Related: [AEO (answer engine optimization)](../glossary#aeo/index.html), [AI SEO](../glossary#ai-seo/index.html), [Citation](../glossary#citation/index.html)

## Knowledge graph

**A database of entities and how they connect, used by search engines and AI to understand facts.**

Google's Knowledge Graph and similar systems link your business to its location, category, people and other facts. A strong presence in these graphs makes it easier for AI to recognize and describe you.

Related: [Entity](../glossary#entity/index.html), [Structured data](../glossary#structured-data/index.html)

## llms.txt

**A proposed plain-text file at the root of a website that points AI systems to its most useful pages.**

llms.txt is a community proposal, not an official standard, and assistants vary in whether they use it. It's quick to add and does no harm. Make one with our [llms.txt generator](../tools/llms-txt-generator/index.html).

Related: [Structured data](../glossary#structured-data/index.html)

## Local AI Blueprint™

**Local AI Registry's done-for-you program that works all 11 signals for a business.**

The Local AI Blueprint™ is one plan, one team and one monthly report covering every signal AI checks. Learn more on the [Blueprint page](../blueprint/index.html) and about [our 90-day guarantee](../guarantee/index.html).

Related: [AI Score](../glossary#ai-score/index.html), [AI visibility](../glossary#ai-visibility/index.html)

## NAP consistency

**Having the same business name, address and phone number everywhere your business is listed.**

NAP stands for name, address, phone. Many practitioners add hours. Inconsistent NAP makes it harder for AI to confirm which listings belong to you. See [directory listings](../signals/directory-listings/index.html).

Related: [Entity](../glossary#entity/index.html), [Citation](../glossary#citation/index.html)

## Schema markup

**Code added to a web page that labels facts, such as your business name, hours, services and reviews, in a standard vocabulary.**

Schema markup uses the shared vocabulary at schema.org, usually written as JSON-LD. It doesn't change how a page looks; it tells machines exactly what the page is about. Build yours with our free [schema generator](../tools/schema-generator/index.html).

Related: [Structured data](../glossary#structured-data/index.html), [Entity](../glossary#entity/index.html)

## Structured data

**Information organized in a fixed format machines can read without interpretation.**

Schema markup is the most common kind of structured data on websites. Business listings, menus and inventory feeds are others. The more of your key facts exist as structured data, the less AI has to guess.

Related: [Schema markup](../glossary#schema-markup/index.html), [Knowledge graph](../glossary#knowledge-graph/index.html)

# How to get your local business recommended by AI

> How to get your local business recommended by ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI: how assistants decide, the 8 steps in order, and the 11 signals behind every.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/guide/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

The complete guide

By [Steve Lee](../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** AI assistants recommend the local businesses they can confirm from many trusted sources. First make sure AI can find you: let OpenAI’s crawler read your site, claim Bing Places and claim your business in ChatGPT. Then make your details identical everywhere, complete your Google profile, build steady reviews, give each service a clear page, get onto the lists and articles AI reads, and check what each assistant says every month.

## How AI decides which local business to recommend

When someone asks ChatGPT "who's the best dentist near me?" or asks Google's AI for a plumber who can come today, the assistant doesn't hold a ranked list of every business. It looks the question up, reads what it can find, and names the few businesses it is most confident about.

Confidence comes from agreement. If your website, your Google profile, three review sites, a local news story and a best-of list all describe the same business at the same address doing the same thing, the assistant can name you without worrying it's wrong. If your details conflict, your reviews are thin and nobody else mentions you, it plays it safe and names someone else.

So the job isn't to trick an algorithm. It's to make your business the easiest one in your area to confirm.

From our AI Answer Watch

- We asked ChatGPT “best rhinoplasty surgeon in [city]” six times in each of 10 US cities on one afternoon, Nov 13, 2026. Only 2 of the 10 cities got the same #1 every time.
- A narrower question gave a steadier answer: for “best closed rhinoplasty surgeon in Los Angeles,” ChatGPT named the same surgeon in all three runs.
- So measure how often AI names you across repeated asks, not where you land in one screenshot.

[See every screenshot in AI Answer Watch](../answer-watch/index.html)

New data from our research team

**73%**

73% of the 128,400+ local businesses Local AI Registry has scored are named by zero AI assistants (our estimate from AI-visibility checks). [Local AI Registry data](../methodology/index.html)

**76.4%**

Local business searches triggered a Google AI Overview 76.4% of the time, compared with 13.7% of all searches. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

**67.5%**

News outlets supplied 67.5% of the citations in Google's AI answers about local businesses. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

## Start here: the three steps ChatGPT itself gives

On Nov 13, 2026 we asked ChatGPT "how do I get my local business recommended by ChatGPT?" Its first steps weren't about content or links. They were about making sure it can find and read your business at all. Do these first; each takes minutes.

1. **Let ChatGPT read your website** ChatGPT finds websites with OpenAI's search crawler, called OAI-SearchBot. If your site blocks it, ChatGPT can't cite your pages. Ask whoever runs your site to check the `robots.txt` file allows it:

   ```
   User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
   Allow: /
   ```

   Also check that your hosting or security firewall isn't blocking it. OpenAI lists its crawlers in [its crawler documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots).
2. **Claim your business on Bing Places** Microsoft's Copilot answers from Bing, and ChatGPT tells owners to set up Bing Places alongside Google. It's free at [bingplaces.com](https://www.bingplaces.com/), and you can import your Google profile so the details match exactly.
3. **Claim your business in ChatGPT** OpenAI's Business Hub lets you claim your listing inside ChatGPT, correct your details, get a verified badge and see how often ChatGPT shows you. [Step-by-step: claim your business in ChatGPT](../guide/claim-your-business-in-chatgpt/index.html).

With those done, AI can find you. The eight steps below are what make it choose you.

## The 8 steps, in order

1. **See where you stand** Ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Google the questions your customers ask, with your city. Write down who is named and which sources each assistant cites. Those sources are your map. The [prompt finder](../tools/prompt-finder/index.html) gives you the questions; a [free check](../tools/ai-visibility-check/index.html) does it with you.
2. **Make your facts identical everywhere** Same name, address, phone and hours on your site, your Google profile and every directory. This is the foundation every other step depends on. [Directory listings guide](../signals/directory-listings/index.html).
3. **Complete and activate your Google profile** Right category, every service, weekly posts, real photos. Google's AI and Gemini read it directly; other assistants see it through search. [Google profile guide](../signals/google-profile/index.html).
4. **Build a steady flow of reviews** Ask every customer, on more than one site, and reply to every review. Reviews that name the service are what AI quotes back. [Reputation guide](../signals/reputation/index.html).
5. **Give each service its own clear page** Answer the question in the first two sentences, add an FAQ and structured data. AI can't recommend you for a service your site barely mentions. [Web management guide](../signals/web-management/index.html) and [SEO guide](../signals/seo/index.html).
6. **Get onto the lists and articles AI reads** The sources the assistants cited in step 1 are your outreach list. [Best-of guides](../signals/best-of-guides/index.html), [third-party articles](../signals/third-party-articles/index.html) and [PR](../signals/pr/index.html).
7. **Add video and labeled photos** Short videos that answer customer questions, and photos named and described for what they show. [Video](../signals/video/index.html) and [photo codifying](../signals/photo-codifying/index.html).
8. **Check every month** AI answers change. Repeat step 1 monthly, compare, and work on whatever the winning businesses have that you don't. [AI monitoring guide](../signals/ai-monitoring/index.html).

Prefer one page you can print? Use [the checklist](../guide/checklist/index.html).

# How to claim your business in ChatGPT

> Step by step: how to claim and verify your business in ChatGPT's Business Hub, what it changes, what it doesn't, and five things to check first.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/guide/claim-your-business-in-chatgpt/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

New from OpenAI

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** Sign in to ChatGPT, open Business Hub, find your business and verify it by phone, business email, website domain or Shopify. After OpenAI approves the claim, verify your identity with Persona to publish changes, get the blue check and see how often ChatGPT shows you. Claiming is free, but it doesn't guarantee ChatGPT will recommend you.

On November 10, 2026, OpenAI opened Businesses in ChatGPT: a way for owners to claim their business inside ChatGPT, keep its details current and see how often ChatGPT shows it. Here's how to do it, step by step, and what it will and won't change.

## How to claim your business in ChatGPT

1. **Sign in and find your business** Sign in to ChatGPT and open Business Hub from the sidebar (or go to [chatgpt.com/business-hub](https://chatgpt.com/business-hub)). Search for your business by name and pick the listing that matches. Local businesses can currently claim only an existing US listing.
2. **Verify that it's yours** Choose one of the methods offered: a code by text or call to your business phone, a code to your business email, a TXT record added to your website's DNS, or your Shopify store. If someone else manages your domain, ask them to add the record.
3. **Wait for approval** OpenAI reviews the claim and emails you its decision or a request for more information.
4. **Verify your identity with Persona** To publish changes, see insights or get the blue check, you complete identity verification with Persona. Have a government ID, business registration details and proof you can represent the business ready. Make sure the name and address match your official records exactly.
5. **Update your details** Add or correct your website, description, category, logo and cover photo. OpenAI reviews changes before they appear, and ChatGPT can still draw on other sources.
6. **Add your team or agency** The admin who claimed the business can add teammates and grant an agency access. Use each person's own ChatGPT account, and never forward a personal claim invitation.

## What claiming does

- You can correct the details ChatGPT shows about you.
- A blue check appears once your Persona verification is approved.
- You see insights for the last 28 days: mentions, website clicks and the topics where you come up. For a local business, a mention counts when ChatGPT shows a result for your location.

## What it doesn't do

OpenAI is clear that claiming "does not guarantee higher placement or sales," and that ChatGPT keeps making its own recommendations. Advertising doesn't change its answers either. ChatGPT still decides from what it reads about you across the web: your reviews, your listings, articles about you and your own site.

**6.5%**

Businesses' own websites supplied just 6.5% of those citations.

## Before you claim: five things to check

- **Your name, address and phone match everywhere.** If your website, Google profile and listings disagree, you're handing ChatGPT a conflict. [Why it matters](../../signals/directory-listings/index.html).
- **Your hours are written out as text** on your site, not only in an image.
- **Your site isn't blocking OpenAI's crawler.** OpenAI says sites must allow OAI-SearchBot to appear in ChatGPT search.
- **Your site has LocalBusiness schema.** [Free schema generator](../../tools/schema-generator/index.html).
- **The person claiming can verify.** Whoever controls the business phone, email or domain should do it, or be there when it's done.

## Frequently asked questions

How do I claim my business in ChatGPT?

Sign in to ChatGPT, open Business Hub, search for your business, choose the matching listing and verify by phone, business email, website domain or Shopify. After OpenAI approves the claim, complete identity verification with Persona to publish changes and see insights.

Is claiming my business in ChatGPT free?

Yes. You don't need an Ads account or an Enterprise agreement to claim an eligible business.

Will claiming make ChatGPT recommend my business?

Not by itself. OpenAI says claiming doesn't guarantee higher placement. ChatGPT still recommends based on what it reads about you across the web.

Can my agency manage my ChatGPT business profile?

Yes. The admin who claimed the business can add teammates and grant an agency access in Business Hub.

Can local businesses outside the US claim a listing?

For now, local stores and restaurants can claim only an existing US listing.

# Why doesn't ChatGPT recommend my business?

> The seven most common reasons ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI don't recommend a local business, and how to find and fix yours.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/guide/not-showing-up/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Troubleshooting

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** Usually because the assistant can't confirm enough about you, or it can confirm more about a competitor. Conflicting details, thin reviews, unclear service pages and no outside mentions are the most common causes.

## The seven most common reasons

01

**Your details conflict across the web**  
If listings show different phones, addresses or names, AI can't be sure which business is real. [How to fix it](../../signals/directory-listings/index.html)

02

**Your reviews are thin or old**  
Fewer, older reviews than nearby competitors make you the riskier recommendation. [How to fix it](../../signals/reputation/index.html)

03

**Your site doesn't clearly say what you do**  
If a service has no page of its own, AI has nothing to quote for it. [How to fix it](../../signals/web-management/index.html)

04

**Nobody else talks about you**  
No articles, lists or press means no outside proof. [How to fix it](../../signals/third-party-articles/index.html)

05

**You're missing from the lists AI reads**  
Assistants often answer "best" questions from local best-of lists. [How to fix it](../../signals/best-of-guides/index.html)

06

**Your Google profile is incomplete**  
Google's AI and Gemini lean on it directly. [How to fix it](../../signals/google-profile/index.html)

07

**The question is too far from what you offer**  
AI matches questions to services. If you never mention a service, you won't be named for it. [How to fix it](../../signals/seo/index.html)

# What Is an AI Score, and How Is It Calculated?

> The AI Score is a 0 to 100 measure of how findable and recommendable a local business is to AI assistants, built from eight published signals.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/journal/what-is-an-ai-score/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Journal

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

---

## What the AI Score measures

The AI Score is a single number, from 0 to 100, that measures how findable and recommendable a local business is to AI assistants like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews. It is the metric we built Local AI Registry around, and we publish exactly how it is calculated. A high score means AI can find you, trust you, and name you when a customer asks; a low score means it cannot.

The number matters because the results are stark. Across the local businesses we have scored, nearly two in three land below 45 out of 100, and barely one in seventy-five clears 65. Most local businesses are not close to being recommendable by AI, and most owners have no idea where they stand.

64%of the local businesses we scored land below 45 out of 100

The AI Score exists to turn that invisible problem into one number you can see, act on, and track. It is the answer to the question every owner now has to ask: [does AI recommend me, and why not?](https://localairegistry.com/journal/how-ai-decides-which-local-business-to-recommend)

## The eight signals behind the score

The AI Score is not a black box or a single-metric gimmick. It is built from eight signals, each measuring a different part of whether an assistant can find and recommend you. Every weight is documented in our [scoring methodology](../../methodology/index.html).

- Retrieval grounding: can AI find and cite you for the queries that drive bookings, not just your brand name.
- Off-property attestation: what independent sources across the web say about you.
- AI visibility: whether specific assistants already name you today.
- Reviews: volume, recency, rating, and whether you respond to them.
- Google Business Profile: how complete and accurate your listing is.
- Authority: the quality of the sites that link to and reference you.
- Speed and mobile: whether your site is technically eligible to be cited.
- Content and schema: whether your pages are clear and machine-readable.

The first two signals, retrieval grounding and off-property attestation, carry the most weight, because they are what actually decide an AI recommendation. The other six are eligibility: necessary, but not sufficient.

## How the number is calculated

Each signal is scored on its own, then combined into the final 0-to-100 number using a weighted geometric mean rather than a simple average. The distinction matters. A geometric mean leans on your weakest signal, so a business cannot paper over a missing off-property presence with a fast website. If any load-bearing signal is near zero, the overall score stays low, which mirrors how an assistant actually behaves: one strong attribute does not earn a recommendation when a critical one is absent.

The weights come from how much each signal moves a real AI recommendation, not from what is easiest to measure. That is why two businesses with identical websites can score very differently: the one the wider web corroborates scores higher, because corroboration is what the assistant grounds its answer in.

## What a good AI Score looks like

Because most local businesses score low, the bar to stand out is lower than it looks. Roughly:

- A score of 65 or above is good: AI can reliably find and recommend you. Very few businesses are here yet.
- A score in the 45 to 64 range is fair: you are eligible and sometimes named, with clear gaps to close.
- Below 45 is poor: AI struggles to find or trust you, and a competitor is getting the recommendation instead.

The point of the number is not the grade, it is the diagnosis. Your AI Score comes with the specific signals dragging it down, so you know what to fix first.

## Why the score is independent

No business can buy a higher AI Score, and no one can pay to be removed from a competitor’s comparison. We [never sell rank](../../trust/index.html), and we publish the method so anyone can check our work. That independence is the whole point: a score you could buy would tell an assistant nothing, and it would tell you nothing either.

## Common questions

### What is a good AI Score?

Broadly, 65 or above is good, 45 to 64 is fair, and below 45 is poor. Because most local businesses currently score below 45, even reaching the fair range puts you ahead of the majority of your competitors.

### Is checking my AI Score free?

Yes. You can look up any business and see its AI Score for nothing.

### How is an AI Score different from a Google ranking?

A Google ranking is your position in a list of blue links. An AI Score measures whether an assistant will name you at all when it answers a question with a single recommendation instead of a list. The signals overlap, but the outcome an AI Score predicts is being the answer, not being on page one.

### Can I improve my AI Score?

Yes, and the score tells you how. It surfaces which of the eight signals are weakest, so you fix the ones that move an AI recommendation first, chiefly retrieval grounding and off-property attestation.

### How often is the AI Score updated?

It reflects the most recent measurement of what assistants say and the underlying signals. As you improve a signal, or as the assistants change, the score is recalculated so it stays a current read rather than a one-time snapshot.

# HIPAA Business Associate Agreement

> Sign Local AI Registry's HIPAA Business Associate Agreement online. For healthcare practices: how we handle any protected health information, in plain language.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/legal/baa/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

For healthcare practices

If you're a healthcare practice, sign our Business Associate Agreement online in about two minutes. We countersign and email you the executed copy within one business day.

### 1. Who this is between

This Business Associate Agreement (the “Agreement”) is between the healthcare practice signing below (the “Covered Entity”) and Blind LLC, a Wyoming limited liability company doing business as Local AI Registry (the “Business Associate”). It applies to any Protected Health Information (“PHI”) the Business Associate creates, receives, maintains or transmits for the Covered Entity while providing its services.

### 2. Definitions

Terms used but not defined here, such as Breach, Designated Record Set, Disclosure, Individual, Minimum Necessary, Protected Health Information, Required by Law, Secretary, Security Incident, Subcontractor, Unsecured Protected Health Information and Use, have the meanings given in the HIPAA Rules at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164.

### 3. What we do and don't touch

Our services (verified business records, Google Business Profile management, review replies, listings, content and AI visibility work) are designed to work without PHI. We do not need patient records and ask that you not send them. If PHI reaches us anyway, for example in a review, a message or a booking request, this Agreement governs how we handle it.

### 4. Our obligations

The Business Associate agrees to: (a) not use or disclose PHI other than as permitted by this Agreement or as Required by Law; (b) use appropriate safeguards, and comply with Subpart C of 45 CFR Part 164 for electronic PHI, to prevent use or disclosure other than as provided here; (c) report to the Covered Entity any use or disclosure not provided for by this Agreement, including Breaches of Unsecured PHI as required by 45 CFR 164.410, and any Security Incident it becomes aware of; (d) ensure that any Subcontractors that create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on its behalf agree to the same restrictions and conditions, in line with 45 CFR 164.502(e)(1)(ii) and 164.308(b)(2); (e) make PHI in a Designated Record Set available as needed for the Covered Entity to meet 45 CFR 164.524; (f) make amendments to PHI in a Designated Record Set as directed under 45 CFR 164.526; (g) keep and provide the information needed for an accounting of disclosures under 45 CFR 164.528; (h) to the extent it carries out a Covered Entity obligation under Subpart E of 45 CFR Part 164, comply with the requirements that apply to the Covered Entity; and (i) make its internal practices, books and records available to the Secretary for determining compliance with the HIPAA Rules.

### 5. Permitted uses and disclosures

The Business Associate may use or disclose PHI only as necessary to perform its services for the Covered Entity, as Required by Law, and for its proper management and administration or to carry out its legal responsibilities, as permitted by 45 CFR 164.504(e)(4). It will follow the Minimum Necessary standard and will not use or disclose PHI in a way that would violate Subpart E of 45 CFR Part 164 if done by the Covered Entity. Review replies are written so they never confirm that a reviewer is a patient.

### 6. Your obligations

The Covered Entity will tell the Business Associate about any limitation in its notice of privacy practices, any change in or revocation of an Individual's permission, and any restriction it has agreed to, to the extent it affects our use or disclosure of PHI. It will not ask us to use or disclose PHI in any way not permitted under the HIPAA Rules if done by the Covered Entity.

### 7. Term and termination

This Agreement starts on the date it is signed and ends when the services end or when either party terminates it. If either party determines the other has violated a material term, it may terminate this Agreement and the related services if the violation is not cured within 30 days. When it ends, the Business Associate will return or destroy all PHI it still holds, or, if that is not feasible, extend these protections to that PHI and limit further use and disclosure for as long as it keeps it.

### 8. General

References to the HIPAA Rules mean the sections as in effect or as amended. The parties will amend this Agreement as needed to comply with the law. Any ambiguity will be read to permit compliance with the HIPAA Rules. This Agreement is governed by the laws of the State of Wyoming, except where federal law controls.

# Privacy Policy

> How Local AI Registry collects, uses, and protects information about you and the businesses we serve, including data accessed via Google Business Profile.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/legal/privacy/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Legal

Section 01

## Introduction

Local AI Registry is a product of **Blind LLC** (“we,” “our,” or “us”). When we say “the Services,” we mean our website at localairegistry.com, the owner dashboards it hosts, the public business profile pages we generate, the review-collection and photo-upload tools we host on your behalf, and the integrations that connect those tools to Google and the other platforms listed below.

By using the Services, you accept the practices described in this policy. If you do not agree, please do not use the Services. We’ll always tell you when this document materially changes (see Section 14).

Section 02

## Information we collect

### Information you give us directly

When you create an account, claim a business, or buy a plan, you provide your name, email address, phone number, business name and address, the services your business offers, and the keywords you want us to track. If you pay for a plan, your card details go directly to our payment processor, we never store or see full card numbers, CVV codes, or bank details.

### Information from the public web and our partners

For every business we surface on the public site, we collect information from Google Maps, public review platforms, business websites we scrape with permission, and SEO data providers (DataForSEO and others listed in Section 7). This includes hours, categories, photos, opening times, popular times, organic keyword rankings, backlinks, and reviews. We compute a Digital Score from these signals.

### Information from connected accounts

When you authorize a paid plan that includes the Google Business Profile integration, we receive access tokens that let us read and (with your approval) write to your listing on your behalf. See Section 4 for exactly what we do with that access, and how to revoke it at any time.

### Information collected automatically

When you visit the public site or your dashboard, we record limited usage information: your IP address (used briefly for spam protection and rate limiting), browser and device type, the pages you view, and how you arrived. We use this to keep the site fast, fix bugs, and protect against abuse.

We log a salted SHA-256 hash of (IP + 30-minute time bucket) on public profile pageviews so business owners can see how many distinct visitors viewed their profile this week without us storing the raw IP. After the bucket window expires, the hash cannot be reversed.

### Customers your business sends to us

If you use our review collection or photo upload tools, your customers may give us their name, rating, written feedback, and photos via your branded link. We process this on your behalf as your service provider; you remain the controller of that data. We do not contact those customers for any reason other than the flow they entered.

Section 03

## How we use your information

We use the information described in Section 2 to:

- Provide, operate, secure, and improve the Services.
- Compute Digital Scores and editorial summaries for every business listed on the public site.
- Deliver the SEO modules you have purchased, including drafting Google Business Profile posts, replying to reviews, building citations, and producing monthly reports.
- Process payments, manage subscriptions, and prevent fraud.
- Send transactional messages: phone verification codes, approval requests, billing receipts, weekly progress digests, and monthly reports.
- Respond to support requests and dispute resolution.
- Comply with legal obligations and enforce our Terms of Service.

We do not sell your personal information. We do not share it for cross-context behavioral advertising. We do not buy advertising profiles to target you.

Section 04

## Google API Services data

Local AI Registry accesses your Google account data only with your explicit OAuth authorization and only for the purposes you sign up for. **Local AI Registry’s use and transfer of information received from Google APIs to any other app will adhere to the [Google API Services User Data Policy](https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy), including the Limited Use requirements.**

### Scopes we may request

Depending on the modules you purchase, we request access to the following Google services:

Sign in with Google
:   Basic profile (name, email, profile photo) so you can log in to Local AI Registry with your Google account.

Google Business Profile
:   Read your business listing details, posts, photos, reviews, and Q&A. Write new posts, photos, and review replies on your behalf when you approve them (or pre-approve them via Auto-Approve in Settings).

### How we use Google data

Google account information is used solely to identify you when you sign in. Google Business Profile data is used to populate your owner dashboard, surface what needs attention, draft content for your approval, and publish that content to your listing after you (or your designated approver) approve it. We do not use Google data to train generalized AI/ML models, and we do not transfer Google data to third parties except the sub-processors strictly necessary to operate the Services (Section 7).

### How to revoke access

You can revoke our access to your Google account at any time at [myaccount.google.com/permissions](https://myaccount.google.com/permissions). When you revoke access, any pending automated actions on your Google Business Profile are cancelled within minutes. The associated tokens are deleted from our systems within 24 hours.

Section 05

## AI-generated content

Local AI Registry uses large language models (OpenAI and Google Gemini, principally) to draft Google Business Profile posts, review replies, FAQ answers, monthly report narratives, and content suggestions. These drafts are generated against your business’s data, your selected brand voice, and your written brand rules.

Every AI-generated artifact that publishes to a public platform passes through an approval gate by default. You can pre-approve specific content types under Settings → Auto-Approve, in which case those drafts ship without per-item review, you remain fully responsible for the published output. We log every draft, every approval, and every publish so you can audit the chain end-to-end from your dashboard.

AI providers may briefly cache prompts and responses for safety and abuse-monitoring purposes per their published policies. We do not authorize providers to use your data for model training, and we use API tiers that contractually prohibit such use where available.

Section 06

## Cookies and similar technologies

Local AI Registry uses a small number of essential cookies: a session cookie when you log in, a CSRF protection cookie, and a preference cookie for any dashboard layout choices you make.

We also use two privacy-respecting analytics tools to understand how the site is used: Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity. They tell us which pages people visit, how they arrive, and where the site is slow or confusing. Microsoft Clarity records anonymized session activity, clicks, scrolls, and page navigation, so we can find and fix bugs and rough edges. We use this only to measure and improve the Services. We do not use advertising cookies, we do not sell your information, and we do not track you across other sites for advertising (see Section 3).

Where we use a third party to deliver part of the Services (a hosted Stripe Checkout page, for example), that third party may set its own cookies on its own domain; their cookie policies govern that use.

Section 07

## Third-party processors

We rely on the sub-processors below to operate the Services. Each one receives only the data needed for its specific function, under a data-processing agreement that restricts re-use. You can request a current list at any time by contacting us.

Stripe
:   Payment processing, subscription billing, customer portal. We send Stripe your email, business name, and the modules you bought.

Twilio
:   Phone-number verification (SMS OTP) and outbound transactional SMS. We send Twilio your phone number and the message to deliver.

Resend
:   Transactional email (verification, approval requests, weekly digests, monthly reports). We send Resend recipient email addresses and message contents.

Google (Cloud, Places, Maps, PageSpeed, Business Profile)
:   Sign-in, location autocomplete, map rendering, site performance scoring, GBP read and write. Data flows are scoped per Section 4.

DataForSEO
:   Keyword ranking data, SERP screenshots, organic traffic estimates, backlink data, review ingestion, business listing data. We send DataForSEO public business identifiers (website, name, address, GBP placeId) and target keywords.

BrightLocal
:   Citation campaign management for paid customers on the Off-Page module. We send BrightLocal the business NAP (name, address, phone) and category data.

OpenAI
:   AI-generated content drafting (posts, replies, summaries, reports). We send OpenAI sanitized prompts containing business context, brand voice notes, and content goals. We use API tiers that prohibit training use of submitted data.

Google Gemini
:   AI-generated content drafting and AI visibility checks. Same handling as OpenAI.

SerpZilla / SerpClix / Adsy / RedPress
:   Off-page module vendors used only for customers actively enrolled in those modules: backlinks, CTR campaigns, press release distribution.

DigitalOcean
:   Application hosting, managed Postgres, object storage (DO Spaces) for photos and report PDFs.

Cloudflare
:   CDN, DDoS protection, bot mitigation in front of public routes.

Sentry
:   Error monitoring. Sentry may capture stack traces and request metadata when our application encounters an error. We scrub personally identifying parameters before sending.

No mobile information will be shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. Information sharing to subcontractors in support services, such as customer service, is permitted. All other use case categories exclude text messaging originator opt-in data and consent; this information will not be shared with any third parties.

Section 08

## When we disclose your information

We disclose information only in these specific circumstances:

- **To deliver the Services.** The sub-processors in Section 7 receive what they need to do their job and nothing more.
- **With your direction.** If you connect Google, or instruct us to publish content, we transmit the corresponding data to those platforms on your behalf.
- **To comply with law.** We may disclose information when required by a valid subpoena, court order, or government request. We push back where the request is overbroad and notify you where we are legally permitted to do so.
- **To protect rights and safety.** Where necessary to investigate fraud, security incidents, or violations of our Terms of Service.
- **Business transfer.** If Blind LLC is acquired or merged, customer data transfers to the acquirer under the same protections.

Section 09

## Data retention

We keep account data for as long as your account is active, plus a short tail to handle disputes, support, and legal obligations. Specifically:

- **Account profile and business data:** kept while the account is active; deleted within 30 days of account closure (or sooner on request).
- **OAuth tokens (Google):** deleted within 24 hours of revocation or account closure.
- **Pageview hashes (Section 2):** raw IP is never persisted; the salted hash is kept for 13 months for week-over-week trend reporting, then purged.
- **Billing records:** retained for 7 years to meet tax and accounting obligations.
- **Application logs:** 30 days, then purged.
- **Public business profile pages** we generate from the public web persist as long as the underlying business is operational. Owners can flag inaccurate data or request removal, see Section 11.

Section 10

## Data security

We protect data with industry-standard controls: TLS in transit, AES-256 at rest in managed Postgres and object storage, encrypted secrets, least-privilege access management, structured access logs, and continuous error monitoring. OAuth tokens are stored encrypted with separate key material. Production database access is restricted to a small set of authorized engineers and audited.

No system is impenetrable, so we maintain an incident-response plan and will notify affected users without undue delay if a breach occurs that materially affects their data.

# Methodology: How the AI Score Is Built

> Eight signals, one number from 0 to 100. The heaviest is whether AI can retrieve you at all. Every input, weight, formula, and source, documented.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/methodology/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Methodology

By [Steve Lee](../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

The thesis

## One number. One mechanism.

AI assistants don’t recommend the closest business, the prettiest website, or whoever paid the most. They recommend a business they can retrieve and recognize as real: one that many independent, trustworthy sources describe the same way.

Because retrieval is the gate everything else passes through, the single heaviest signal is whether you appear in the results an AI model pulls from when it answers. Everything else either earns that retrievability or refines what the AI says once you’re in.

Retrievability isn’t one ranking factor among many. It’s the precondition for all of them.

The weights

## How much each signal weighs.

Eight signals, identical for every business, ordered by how much each one moves an AI recommendation. The single heaviest is whether you can be retrieved at all.

Retrievability and the attestation that earns it are the retrieval tier, together 46% of the score. Nearly half.

It measures how likely AI engines are to recommend a business, and how accurately. The same method scores every business on the registry. Every business is scored the same way, and nobody can pay for a better score. Fair starts at 45, good at 65.

Retrieval tier
26%Retrieval groundingWhether you appear in the ranked results AI retrieves and cites: AI-Overview citations, organic top-10 for your money queries, and the Bing index ChatGPT leans on.
20%Off-property attestationVolume and consistency of what others say about you: YouTube mentions, branded web mentions, third-party “best-of” lists. The cause of retrievability.
14%AI visibilityWhether ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and AI Overviews name you, and whether they name you for the right service.
12%Reviews & responseThe star average is only one input. We also read volume, velocity, the specificity of review language, and response cadence. Specific reviews are what AI quotes verbatim.
8%Backlink & citation authorityDomain authority and editorial quality of the sources that attest to you.
8%Google Business ProfileRequired and recommended fields; update cadence. The listing AI pulls from first.
7%Speed & mobileCore Web Vitals at the 75th percentile, on a real phone.
5%Content freshness & schemaCrawl recency, intent alignment, valid JSON-LD, canonicals.

Methods referenced

## We didn’t invent the math.

Every part of the score is a named, published method, borrowed from information retrieval, index construction, and game theory, and each one is cited.

Fig. 8, Methods composing the AI Score · n = 10 · 3 stages · [full citations](../methodology/index.html#references)

Reading a business page

## What the marks on a business page mean

Every fact on a business page carries one of three marks, and every mark points to a reference at the end of that page.

Confirmedsolid circle
:   From a known source: the business's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Yelp, Healthgrades and RealSelf, a licensing board, or measured by Local AI Registry.

Visitor submittedhollow circle
:   Added or corrected by a person, with the date and how they know, like a phone call or a visit.

AI guesshollow triangle
:   What AI engines like ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity are saying right now. Nobody has confirmed it.

Each row is marked Confirmed, Visitor submitted or AI guess, with where it came from. Each reference names the fact, the source, what kind of source it is, and the date it was checked, with a link and an archived copy so anyone can verify it. Visitor references are dated firsthand accounts. AI guesses record what an AI engine said on that date, not what is true.

How AI reads a business

## How AI decides what to tell you about a med spa

When you ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Google for a med spa, the AI doesn't visit each business. It reads what's already written about it: the business's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Yelp and RealSelf, news stories, licensing boards and directories like ours. Then it repeats what those sources agree on.

That's why AI gets small facts wrong. If Yelp says a place is open Mondays and the website says it isn't, the AI has to pick one. Each business page on the registry lists the answers that disagree with what we've confirmed.

The more sources agree, and the more specific they are, the more confidently AI recommends a business. A review that says "the nurse did half a syringe in my lips and it looks natural" is far more useful to an AI than one that says "great place."

## How AI decides what to tell you about an eye surgery practice

When you ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Google for an eye surgeon, the AI doesn't visit the practice. It reads what's already written about it: the practice's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Healthgrades and Yelp, your state's medical and optometry boards, news stories and directories like ours. Then it repeats what those sources agree on.

That's why AI gets small facts wrong. If one site says a surgeon still operates there and the practice's own website doesn't list them, the AI has to pick one. Each business page on the registry lists the answers that disagree with what we've confirmed.

The more sources agree, and the more specific they are, the more confidently AI recommends a practice. A review that says "my surgeon did my cataract surgery on a Tuesday and I was driving by Friday" is far more useful to an AI than one that says "great doctor."

Ask most Orange County med spas what Botox costs and the answer starts with \"it depends.\" Prices run $10 to $20 a unit, and the bill depends on how many units the injector uses. For the most common treatment, the FDA-labeled 20-unit dose for frown lines, per-unit pricing elsewhere works out to $200 to $400. The studio opened in 2024. It was founded and funded by veterans of the neurotoxin industry, people who spent their careers in product strategy, branding and sales at the companies that make these drugs. Its medical director, Johnathan Slone, MD, is a board-certified surgeon licensed in California who performed thousands of acute-care procedures, including robotic trauma surgery, before turning to injectables. It sits about 1.2 miles from Hoag Hospital Newport Beach, 2.3 miles from the Newport Beach Pier and about 4 miles from South Coast Plaza and John Wayne Airport, which makes it a short drive for anyone living or working around the 17th Street shops, Newport Heights or the airport business district. TIEV Med Spa, with 206 Yelp reviews, offers the richest memberships, and GLO Bar MedSpa pairs Botox with laser skin treatments. QUIKTOX was named best value. The trade-offs are real. ## Take it off the registry.

You can ask us to remove a business from the public registry. If you only need to fix a detail, it’s usually better to [report an error](../report-an-error/index.html)

# The Convergence

> White Paper 03 from Local AI Registry Research reads eleven independent streams of evidence on how local businesses get recommended by AI, explained twice.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/proof/the-convergence-white-paper/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

White paper 03

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

---

## How to read this report

### The view from above, and how it's written

Most research on AI search reports one study at a time. This report does the opposite. It gathers every bucket of evidence we could find on how local businesses get recommended by AI, lays them on one table, and steps back until the whole picture resolves. From that altitude, the disconnected facts collapse into a single conclusion and four currents that run beneath all of them.

Because the goal is to be useful to a business owner and defensible to a skeptic, every section is written twice. In Plain Terms states the point in language anyone can act on. The Proof then establishes it rigorously, naming the specific researcher, study, court record, or dataset behind each claim, with the chart that shows it.

### How every claim is labelled

- **CITED** A figure from a named, linkable source. Real or omitted, never invented.
- **ANALYSIS** Our own conclusion from reading the sources together.
- **PROJECTION** A forward inference from a measured trend. Flagged, never disguised as data.

## I · The Convergence, eleven streams, one substrate

### In Plain Terms

We pulled together every kind of evidence we could find about how AI decides which local businesses to recommend, what shoppers do, what the data shows, what Google's own people and documents say, what scientists have proven about how these systems retrieve information, and what the law now requires. They come from totally different places and were never meant to be read together. But when you put them side by side, they all say the same thing: AI doesn't recommend a website, a profile, or whoever is closest. It recommends a business it can recognize as real, one that many trustworthy sources independently describe the same way. Being that recognizable, verifiable business is the whole game.

### The Proof

The diagram below places eleven independent research streams around a single center. Each was produced by different people, with different methods, for different reasons. Read individually they are a pile of disconnected facts. Read together they converge, every one of them describes, from its own angle, the same underlying object: the verifiable entity.

**Figure I · The convergence.** Eleven independent streams; each source named below and in References.

Here is who and what each stream is, and what it independently establishes **CITED**, the named evidence behind the picture:

**BrightLocal.** Local Consumer Review Survey 2026. 45% of consumers now use AI for local discovery (up from 6%), and 88% fact-check the result, so people seek, then verify, a recommendation.¹

45%of consumers now use AI for local discovery (up from 6%). CITED: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey 2026.
88%fact-check the result. CITED: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey 2026.

**Glenn Allsopp · Ahrefs.** 75,000-brand visibility study. The top correlate of AI visibility is YouTube and branded web mentions (0.737), not links or pages, the signal is off-site, distributed conversation.²

0.737The top correlate of AI visibility is YouTube and branded web mentions. CITED: Glenn Allsopp, Ahrefs, 75,000-brand visibility study.

**Ahrefs · 146M SERPs.** AI Overview trigger study. Specific, conversational, entity-rich questions trigger AI answers far more than bare keywords (57.9% vs 9.5%).³

57.9%full question-style queries trigger an AI Overview. CITED: Ahrefs, What Triggers AI Overviews? 86 Factors, 146M SERPs.
9.5%single-word searches trigger an AI Overview. CITED: Ahrefs, What Triggers AI Overviews? 86 Factors, 146M SERPs.

**Local Falcon.** ~60,000 simulations. Distance from the searcher correlates with AI rank at r = 0.001, proximity, the old master variable, is gone; what remains is authority.⁵

r = 0.001Distance from the searcher correlates with AI rank. CITED: Local Falcon, AI Overviews proximity whitepaper, ~60,000 simulations.

**Seer Interactive.** Citation analysis. The AI assembles answers by quoting other sources about a business; ChatGPT matches Bing's results 87% of the time.⁶

87%ChatGPT matches Bing's results. CITED: Seer Interactive, SearchGPT/Bing citation & CTR analyses.

**Sensor Tower.** State of AI 2026. The assistant market is fragmenting (ChatGPT 46%, Gemini 28%), yet every assistant grounds answers in retrieved, attested sources the same way.⁷

46%ChatGPT. CITED: Sensor Tower, State of AI 2026.
28%Gemini. CITED: Sensor Tower, State of AI 2026.

**Darren Shaw · Whitespark.** Local Search Ranking Factors 2026. Even the classic local pack is shifting weight toward reviews, third-party attestation, now 16% and rising.⁸

16%Even the classic local pack is shifting weight toward reviews. CITED: Darren Shaw, Whitespark, Local Search Ranking Factors 2026.

**Google + Judge Mehta.** Search Central docs; U.S. v. Google. Robby Stein describes "query fan-out"; court filings disclose FastSearch/RankEmbed, semantic retrieval of entities, not link-counting.⁹,¹²,¹⁷

**Retrieval science.** Peer-reviewed literature. Aggarwal (Princeton), Dai, Fayyaz, Yamada (LUKE): retrievers reward prominent, well-grounded, verifiable entities.¹⁹,²⁵,²⁶,³⁰

**FTC + European Commission.** Consumer Review Rule; EU AI Act. Fabricated attestation is now illegal ($53,088/violation), only genuine signals are durable.³⁵,³⁸

$53,088per violation: fabricated attestation is now illegal. CITED: U.S. FTC, Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR 465.

**Field reports.** Owners & local SEOs. Businesses surface in AI without buying placement, and mentions lift then decay (Andrew Shotland), exactly as a click-trained retriever predicts.⁴¹

> Eleven instruments, eleven methods, one reading: AI local visibility is won as a verifiable entity, attested consistently across independent sources.

That single substrate is the bird's-eye finding. Everything that follows, the four currents, is simply what this convergence does to a local business, and the one thing the whole landscape is still missing.

## II · Current One, the battlefield left your property

**It's no longer about what you publish**

### In Plain Terms

For twenty years, "doing your SEO" meant working on things you owned: your website, your pages, your Google profile. That era is ending. The things that now make AI recommend you mostly live off your own property, what other people say about you on YouTube, in reviews, in community threads, in local round-ups. You've gone from building your storefront to earning a reputation you don't fully control. The job is no longer to publish more about yourself; it's to be talked about, consistently, by others.

### The Proof

Glenn Allsopp's Ahrefs analysis of 75,000 brands ranked every candidate signal by how strongly it correlates with AI visibility. The signals describing what others say about you, YouTube mentions (0.737), branded web mentions (0.66-0.71), sit at the top. The signals describing what you publish about yourself, your domain rating (0.266), the backlinks you build (0.218), the pages you publish (0.194), sit at the bottom.² The gap is not subtle.

0.66-0.71branded web mentions. CITED: Glenn Allsopp, Ahrefs, AI visibility study, 75,000 brands.
0.266your domain rating. CITED: Glenn Allsopp, Ahrefs, AI visibility study, 75,000 brands.
0.218the backlinks you build. CITED: Glenn Allsopp, Ahrefs, AI visibility study, 75,000 brands.
0.194the pages you publish. CITED: Glenn Allsopp, Ahrefs, AI visibility study, 75,000 brands.

**Figure II · Off-property signals win.** Ahrefs, 75,000 brands (Glenn Allsopp), 2026.

The mechanism, disclosed in Judge Amit Mehta's November 2025 ruling in U.S. v. Google, explains why. Google grounds its Gemini answers through a retriever called FastSearch, built on a deep-learning model, RankEmbed, that matches queries to documents semantically rather than by counting links.¹⁷ Google's own VP of Search, Robby Stein, describes the front end as "query fan-out", the model issues dozens of background searches and synthesizes what it retrieves.¹² Neither process rewards a business for publishing more pages about itself; both reward a business that the wider web independently corroborates. **ANALYSIS** The practical relocation is total: the battlefield moved from your domain to the ecosystem's consensus about you.

## III · Current Two, specificity is rewarded at every layer

**Generic loses; specific wins, everywhere**

### In Plain Terms

The single most repeated pattern across all the evidence is this: the more specific you are, the more AI rewards you, and it shows up at every level. Specific questions get AI answers more often than vague searches. First-hand, specific content beats generic listicles. A review that names exactly what you did ("great with anxious dogs") is worth more than a bare five stars. And a business known for one clear thing beats one that claims to do everything. Being known for the right thing isn't a tagline, it's the rule the whole system runs on.

### The Proof

The same generic-to-specific gradient appears independently at four layers. At the query layer, Ahrefs' study of 146 million SERPs shows single-word searches trigger an AI Overview 9.5% of the time, while full question-style queries trigger 57.9%.³ At the content layer, Google's own Search Central guidance explicitly rewards "non-commodity content" and first-hand experience over generic aggregation.¹⁰ At the review layer, AI answers quote the specific language of reviews verbatim, the named service, not the star count. At the entity layer, the retrieval-science consensus (LUKE-style entity grounding) favors precisely-described, unambiguous entities.³⁰

**Figure III · The specificity ladder.** Query: Ahrefs. Content: Google. Review/entity: platform mechanics & LAIR analysis.

This is the academic and mechanical basis for Local AI Registry's founding principle, alignment, not coverage. **ANALYSIS** A business fails in AI not by being invisible but by being known for the wrong, generic thing. The corrective is specificity, applied deliberately at all four layers at once.

## IV · Current Three, four clocks, one transition window

**Four unrelated timers strike at once**

### In Plain Terms

Four completely separate things are all changing at the same moment, roughly 2026 into 2027. How many people use AI for local search. How open AI is to recommending smaller businesses. How people phrase their searches. And when the new AI transparency laws kick in. None of these has anything to do with the others, which is exactly why their lining up matters. When four unrelated clocks all strike the same hour, that's not coincidence; it's a transition. The businesses that move during the window get an advantage the latecomers won't.

### The Proof

Four independently-measured trends converge on the same window. Adoption: BrightLocal records consumer use of AI for local discovery rising from 6% to 45% across 2025-26.¹ The citation window: Ahrefs finds the share of AI-Overview citations drawn from the organic top ten fell from ~76% to ~38%, widening the pool to the long tail, a window the retrieval-bias literature predicts will re-narrow.⁴,²⁵ The exposure runway: as phrasing turns conversational, local AI-trigger rates climb off their 7.9% floor toward the 57.9% question rate.³ Regulation: the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties take effect 2 August 2026.³⁸

6% to 45%consumer use of AI for local discovery across 2025-26. CITED: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey 2026.
~76% to ~38%the share of AI-Overview citations drawn from the organic top ten. CITED: Ahrefs, 38% of AI Overview Citations Pull From the Top 10.
7.9%the local AI-trigger rate floor. CITED: Ahrefs, What Triggers AI Overviews? 86 Factors, 146M SERPs.
2 August 2026the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties take effect. CITED: European Commission, EU AI Act, Article 50.

**Figure IV · Four clocks, one transition.** BrightLocal; Ahrefs; European Commission. Convergence framing is analysis. ** PROJECTION**

The convergence itself is the argument. **ANALYSIS** Any one trend could be dismissed as noise; four unrelated research streams agreeing on a transition date is a structural signal that the ground is shifting now, and that early, consistent action dominates a wait-and-see posture.

## V · Current Four, the accountability vacuum

**The Keystone · No one can tell you what the AI says**

### In Plain Terms

Here's the strangest part. Everything above says your AI reputation now matters enormously, but nobody can actually tell you what it is. Ask the same question twice and the AI gives different answers. The platforms don't report which businesses they recommend or why. There's no record that follows you across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google. And the law polices AI that lies to customers, not AI that's wrong about you. So the one thing that now decides whether customers find you is the one thing no one is keeping score of. That gap is the whole reason a registry needs to exist.

### The Proof

Four properties you would expect of any system of record are absent across every major AI surface. Reproducibility: practitioners document that AI Overview results "aren't repeatable" run-to-run, and Google's own Search Console does not separate AI-driven clicks. Accuracy: Nelson Liu and Percy Liang (Stanford) found only 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations, and the Tow Center at Columbia found leading AI search tools wrong on more than 60% of queries.³²,³⁴ Cross-platform record: none exists. Regulatory scope: the FTC and EU AI Act target deception of consumers, not accuracy about third-party businesses.³⁵,³⁸

51.5%of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations. CITED: N. F. Liu, T. Zhang, P. Liang (Stanford), Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines.
More than 60%of queries: leading AI search tools wrong. CITED: Tow Center at Columbia, AI Search Has a Citation Problem.

**Figure V · The accountability vacuum.** LAIR analysis of platform reporting, reproducibility & regulatory scope, 2026.

This is the keystone the other three currents rest on. **ANALYSIS** The entire body of evidence converges on "be a verifiable entity," moving fast, on a closing clock, while no neutral party measures whether you are one, reproducibly, across platforms, over time. That negative space, visible only when all eleven streams are held in one frame, is not a gap in the research. It is a description of an institution that does not yet exist.

## VI · The Instrument, what the vacuum implies

If the evidence converges on a substrate no one is measuring, the implied object is not a tactic or a tool, it is an institution: an independent, reproducible record of what AI says about local businesses, and whether they are known for the right things.

That is the function Local AI Registry performs. It scores independent local businesses across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews; it measures not just whether a business is named but whether it is named for the right service, the alignment this report shows the whole system rewards; and it does so repeatedly, across platforms, over time, which is exactly the reproducibility the landscape lacks. The registry is not a product appended to the research. It is the instrument the convergence implies.

### From reading to record

A reader can act on the four currents today: move the work off-property, apply specificity at every layer, act within the window, and treat verifiability as a conversion advantage. But to know where you stand, what you're named for, what you're invisible for, where the reputation and the marketing diverge, requires the instrument. That is what the next page offers.

## VII · The evidence layer, seven findings underneath

**Seven findings underneath the view**

The bird's-eye view is built on a deeper layer of cross-source findings, each one a conclusion drawn by overlaying two or three datasets that none of them states alone. They are summarized here as the supporting evidence beneath the four currents; each is documented at length in companion analysis.

### The seven triangulated findings beneath the convergence

- **01 · The Broken Scoreboard.** The canonical local-pack model and AI visibility are nearly orthogonal. Built from: Ahrefs × Whitespark × antitrust.
- **02 · The Exposure Runway.** The 7.9% local AI rate is a countdown toward the 57.9% question rate. Built from: Ahrefs × BrightLocal.
- **03 · Re-Centralization.** Proximity's death plus prominence bias tilts AI toward incumbents. Built from: Local Falcon × retrieval-bias research.
- **04 · The Closing Window.** A temporary long-tail citation opening that bias predicts will re-narrow. Built from: Ahrefs × field experiment × academia.
- **05 · Reviews Are the Keystone.** The only lever that is ranking signal, citation source, safeguard & legal moat at once. Built from: Whitespark × mechanism × Liu × FTC.
- **06 · The Verification Dividend.** The fact-check, not the recommendation, is where the funnel breaks. Built from: BrightLocal × Tow Center.
- **07 · Two Disjoint Games.** ChatGPT-via-Bing visibility is the underpriced channel. Built from: Seer × Ahrefs × Sensor Tower.

Each finding is graded **ANALYSIS**, a strong hypothesis from real, cited inputs, not a measured fact. Several become measurable original statistics when cross-checked against the live index; those measurements will be published when complete.
