## Methodology & limitations

### How this report was built

This is a work of synthesis at altitude: eleven independent evidence streams, read together to surface the conclusions that only their overlap reveals. Every input is a real, cited figure from a named source; the convergence and the four currents are our own **ANALYSIS**; forward inferences are marked ** PROJECTION**. We hold a strict "real or omitted" rule, no quote, statistic, study, court finding, or researcher is invented, and unverifiable figures (such as a widely-shared "797,444 impressions, 7 clicks" anecdote) are excluded rather than repeated.

### What this method can and cannot claim

Convergence is strong evidence, not proof of mechanism. Many independent sources agreeing on a substrate is a powerful signal, but several inputs are correlational and inherit that limit. Projections are reasoned, not certain, the transition window and the runway are extrapolations from measured trends, flagged as such. The local-AI research gap is real: little peer-reviewed work studies local-business inclusion in AI answers directly, so local conclusions are careful inferences from adjacent retrieval, bias, and entity-grounding research. Vendor incentive exists in some sources; figures were cross-checked where possible. The accountability vacuum is, by definition, where measurement is thinnest, which is precisely the gap the registry is built to close, and why proprietary figures are shown as forthcoming rather than asserted.

Reference numbers are shared across the Local AI Visibility Series for cross-referencing; gaps indicate sources cited in companion papers.

ChatGPT has more than 900 million weekly users, Google’s AI Mode passed one billion monthly users in May 2026 with queries more than doubling every quarter, and Local AI Registry found that 76.4% of local business searches show a Google AI answer before any link.

### What is Local AI Registry Research?

Local AI Registry Research is the research program of Local AI Registry, an answer engine optimization (AEO) company for local businesses. Its dedicated local AI research team studies how ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot find, read and recommend local businesses, and publishes the findings free at localairegistry.com/research.

### What has Local AI Registry’s research found?

In The Local Answer Gap, Local AI Registry analyzed 7,583 Google AI Overviews and 98,020 fact-checked claims. News outlets supplied 67.5% of the citations in AI answers about local businesses, businesses’ own websites supplied 6.5%, and 83.6% of answers told people to check with their local store.

# How Often AI Recommends Your Business

> Local AI Registry reviews 14 sources: ask AI the same thing twice and Gemini’s sources overlap by only 0.46. How to measure how often AI recommends you.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

Research

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

## Key findings

1. In research reviewed by Local AI Registry, the same query run twice shared 0.78 of its sources on Google Search, 0.66 on Google AI Overviews and 0.46 on Gemini (Grossman et al., SIGIR 2026).
2. In a preprint census of cafés, restaurants and bars in Bali reviewed by Local AI Registry, the overlap between repeated runs of the same query ranged from 0.45 for Gemini to 0.22 for Claude.
3. When ChatGPT was asked the same local question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both, according to 8ight.AI data reviewed by Local AI Registry.
4. Only 10.8% of doctors named by an AI model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city, versus 63.9% with web search on, in a preprint audit of the 100 largest US metro areas reviewed by Local AI Registry.
5. Wording changes who AI recommends: 74.7% of the people recommended for “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, versus 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts,” in a peer-reviewed study reviewed by Local AI Registry.
6. ChatGPT declined to recommend an orthopedic surgeon in 52.8% of 40,500 persona-based requests, and stated income, insurance status and location were the strongest predictors of a recommendation, according to research reviewed by Local AI Registry.
7. Only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named in localized searches appeared at every point tested across a town, according to BrightLocal’s 2026 analysis reviewed by Local AI Registry.
8. In the Bali census reviewed by Local AI Registry, 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any of the four AI systems, and being named was associated with documentation such as a website, more reviews, listed prices and mentions elsewhere on the web.
9. Local AI Registry calculated that a business named in 40% of AI answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100, so one answer cannot measure AI visibility.

## What is AI visibility, and why can’t one answer measure it?

Visibility in AI-generated local recommendations is best measured as how often a business is named under stated conditions. A single answer is a genuine observation, but on its own it cannot reliably estimate that frequency.

Consumers are adopting generative assistants for local decisions at speed. In BrightLocal’s 2026 survey of 1,002 US consumers, 45% reported using ChatGPT or another generative AI tool to find local businesses, up from 6% a year earlier.[1](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-1) As the behavior has spread, so has an informal method of judging it. An owner, marketer or analyst asks an assistant for the best provider in a category and city, and reads the reply as a verdict on where a business stands.

That reading carries over an assumption from conventional search, where a page of results could reasonably be treated as a ranking. A generative assistant does not return a stored list. It composes an answer at the moment of the request, from whatever it retrieves and infers under that request’s particular conditions. The research reviewed here points to a different unit of analysis.

### Terms used in this brief

AI visibility
:   How often, how prominently and how accurately a business is named in AI answers, measured as a rate across many answers to the same question.

Recommendation frequency
:   The share of AI answers that name a business under a stated set of systems, configurations, locations, phrasings and dates.

Answer engine optimization (AEO)
:   Making a business’s facts clear, consistent and machine-readable so AI systems include it accurately in their answers.

Generative engine optimization (GEO)
:   The academic term for optimizing content to be cited by generative AI search engines; used interchangeably with AEO.

Overlap (Jaccard similarity)
:   What two runs returned in both, divided by what they returned in either. 1 means identical results; 0 means nothing in common.

Confidence interval
:   The range that likely contains the true rate. A 95% interval only becomes narrow after many answers have been collected.

Web search (grounding)
:   When an AI assistant searches the web during a request instead of answering only from what its model learned in training.

Algorithm audit
:   A way to study a system that cannot be inspected directly, by querying it repeatedly and recording what it returns.

Preprint
:   A research paper shared publicly before peer review.

## Does AI recommend the same businesses every time you ask?

No. When the same query was run twice, Gemini’s sources overlapped by only 0.46, and in a census of Bali venues, Claude’s repeated local recommendations overlapped by just 0.22.

Variation in search results is not new. In a 2015 measurement study of Google Search, Kliman-Silver and colleagues found that 18% to 34% of results for local queries changed with the searcher’s location, and that local queries were also the noisiest category when repeated from the same place at the same time.[2](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-2) Generative systems add another layer of variability, because the answer is written rather than retrieved.

The clearest controlled comparison is a study presented at ACM SIGIR 2026 that examined Google Search, Google’s AI Overviews and Gemini on more than 11,000 real user queries.[3](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-3) When the same query was run twice, the overlap between the sources each system drew on, measured by Jaccard similarity, was 0.78 for conventional Search, 0.66 for AI Overviews and 0.46 for Gemini. Minor edits to a query, such as expanding a contraction or adding a question mark, reduced the rank-weighted similarity of AI Overview sources by 29%, compared with 14% for conventional Search.

Audits of local recommendations show the same pattern in the businesses named. A pre-registered census of every café, restaurant and bar in two Bali submarkets, conducted by a company that sells AI-visibility tools, collected 2,208 answers from four assistants over seven days.[4](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-4) Overlap between repeated runs of the same query ranged from 0.22 for Claude to 0.45 for Gemini. The study’s most consequential finding concerns time. When the queries were repeated two weeks later, overlap with the original answers (0.375) was comparable to overlap between reruns within the same period, and the author attributes most of the variation to sampling rather than drift.

**Figure 1. Ask the same question twice and Gemini's sources overlap by only 0.46, versus 0.78 for Google Search.** When the same query was run twice, the sources Google Search drew on overlapped by 0.78, Google AI Overviews by 0.66 and Gemini by 0.46 (Grossman et al., SIGIR 2026). In a separate preprint census of Bali venues, the local businesses named overlapped by 0.45 for Gemini down to 0.22 for Claude (Pitenin, 2026). Compare bars within a panel, not across panels. Embed this figure

The distinction matters for measurement. If answers drifted steadily, the most recent answer would be an imperfect but current reading. If answers instead scatter around a relatively stable underlying tendency, as this evidence suggests, the tendency is the quantity worth estimating. Each answer is one observation of it, and only an accumulation of observations can show how strong it is.

AEO takeaway

One AI answer is a snapshot, not a ranking.

### What to do

Do not judge your AI visibility from one screenshot. Ask the same customer questions several times, on more than one assistant, and count how often your business is named.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s AI visibility audit shows how a business appears in AI answers today, where answers are wrong, and what competitors are cited for.

## What changes which business AI recommends?

Four conditions: the AI system and its settings, the place, the wording of the request, and time. With web search on, 63.9% of the doctors an AI model named matched a real clinician in the queried city, versus 10.8% with it off.

There is no single frequency. A business can be named often under some conditions and rarely under others. The literature identifies four sets of conditions that change the answer, and a credible measurement has to state which of them it holds fixed.

**Figure 2. Four conditions change which business AI recommends: real local doctors named rose from 10.8% to 63.9% with web search on.** System and configuration, place, wording and time each changed AI recommendations in published research. Each mini-chart comes from a different study and metric, so read each one on its own, not across quadrants. Findings selected and grouped by Local AI Registry. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/images/four-conditions-that-change-which-business-ai-recommends.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/images/four-conditions-that-change-which-business-ai-recommends.png) · [Phone SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/images/four-conditions-that-change-which-business-ai-recommends-mobile.svg)

Data behind this chart

| Condition | Finding | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| System and configuration | Doctors matching a real clinician in the queried city, web search off vs on (same model) | 10.8% vs 63.9% | Ibrahim & Zaki, 2026 (preprint) |
| System and configuration | Sources shared by AI Overviews and Gemini, “near me” queries (overlap) | 0.07 | Grossman et al., 2026 |
| Place | Real doctors named without web search, largest vs smallest third of US metro areas | 16.3% vs 9.5% | Ibrahim & Zaki, 2026 (preprint) |
| Place | Businesses ChatGPT named that appeared at every point tested across a town | 3.5% | BrightLocal, 2026 (industry) |
| Wording and context | Oculoplastic specialists recommended: “an oculoplastic surgeon” vs “a doctor who does eyelid lifts” | 74.7% vs 46.6% | Parikh et al., 2024 |
| Wording and context | ChatGPT responses declining to recommend an orthopedic surgeon | 52.8% | Haupt et al., 2026 |
| Time | Overlap with answers collected two weeks later | 0.375 | Pitenin, 2026 (preprint) |
| Time | Businesses named in either of two ChatGPT answers about 39 minutes apart that appeared in both (median) | 29% | 8ight.AI, 2026 (industry) |

Embed this figure

**System and configuration.** The assistant, the model behind it and whether it searches the web during the request all change the outcome. In an audit of provider recommendations across the 100 largest US metropolitan areas, Ibrahim and Zaki found that only 10.8% of doctors named by a proprietary model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city; with search enabled, the same model reached 63.9%.[5](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-5) Systems also draw on different evidence. For “near me” queries in the SIGIR study, the overlap between sources used by AI Overviews and Gemini was 0.07.[3](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-3) Disagreement between platforms predates generative AI: Li and Hecht found that Google Maps ratings averaged about 0.7 stars higher than Yelp ratings for the same restaurants, and that the two platforms’ top-ten lists for a metropolitan area overlapped little.[6](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-6)

**Place.** Location operates at more than one scale. Between cities, Ibrahim and Zaki found that without search the share of real doctors named fell from 16.3% in the largest third of metropolitan areas to 9.5% in the smallest, a gradient that largely disappeared once search was enabled.[5](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-5) Haupt and colleagues found ChatGPT more likely to recommend an orthopedic surgeon for prompts set in New York City and Chicago than in Phoenix and Houston.[7](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-7) Within a single town, BrightLocal’s 2026 analysis of localized searches found that only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named appeared at every point tested across the area.[8](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-8) Location effects are not uniform, however. For a stratified sample of general queries, the SIGIR study found that moving AI Overview requests from Newark to Austin reduced source similarity by only 0.01 to 0.02 relative to repeated runs from the same place.[3](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-3) How much place matters appears to depend on the system and the kind of question.

**Wording and context.** The words in a request, and what it reveals about the person asking, change who is named. In a peer-reviewed study of chatbot recommendations for oculoplastic surgeons in the 20 largest US cities, 74.7% of the individuals recommended in response to “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, compared with 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts.”[9](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-9) Haupt and colleagues submitted 40,500 persona-based requests for orthopedic surgeons to ChatGPT. It declined to recommend anyone in 52.8% of responses, and stated income, insurance status and location were the strongest predictors of whether a recommendation was given.[7](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-7) Research on brand recommendations points the same way: language models recommended luxury gifts disproportionately to people from high-income countries.[10](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-10)

**Time.** Repetition alone changes answers, as both the SIGIR study and the Bali census show, and it does so over short intervals. 8ight.AI’s 2026 study of local trades found that when ChatGPT was asked the same question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both.[11](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-11) Over longer periods the systems themselves change, as model versions, retrieval sources and defaults are updated, which is why studies such as Parikh’s describe their findings as a record of a single point in time.[9](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-9)

AEO takeaway

State the conditions, or the number means nothing.

### What to do

When you check what AI says about your business, write down the assistant, whether it searched the web, the city, the exact wording and the date, and keep them the same when you check again.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry keeps an owner-confirmed public record of each business, so assistants that search the web find the same verified facts every time they look.

## What can AI visibility research prove, and what can’t it?

It can show how often, and under which conditions, a business is named. It cannot show why. Only 51.5% of sentences written by generative search engines were fully supported by their citations, and 38.3% of ChatGPT’s surgeon suggestions in one study were excluded on review.

Three limits shape what any measurement of AI visibility can claim.

The first is that being named and being named first appear to be different outcomes. In the Bali census, 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any of the four systems. Inclusion was associated with documentation, including having a website, more reviews, listed prices and mentions elsewhere on the web, while star rating was associated only with whether a venue was named first.[4](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-4) These are associations from one hospitality market, reported by a vendor-funded study, but they caution against collapsing inclusion and order into a single rank.

The second is that the sources an assistant displays are imperfect evidence of what produced its answer. In a peer-reviewed audit of four generative search engines, Liu, Zhang and Liang found that only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, and only 74.5% of citations supported the sentence to which they were attached.[12](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-12) Citation patterns can indicate which sources are prominent in a category. They cannot establish cause.

The third is that a name in an answer is not necessarily a correct name. In the 2023 oculoplastic study, 38.3% of ChatGPT’s suggestions were excluded on review; across the three chatbots studied, the most common reasons were a provider practicing in a different city or not existing at all.[9](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-9) In the orthopedic study, 44.6% of recommended surgeons in a coded subset were valid.[7](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-7) Counting mentions without verifying them can overstate visibility, and in healthcare the cost of that error falls on patients as well as practices.

Underlying all three is a broader point: visibility is partly defined by the instrument that measures it. The foundational paper on generative engine optimization (GEO), the research term for what practitioners call answer engine optimization (AEO), measured visibility with explicitly defined impression metrics and reported that content changes raised it by up to 40% on its benchmark, with effects that varied by domain.[13](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-13) Findings of this kind show that visibility in generative answers responds to content. They do not show that a particular change will produce recommendations, or customers, for a particular business.

AEO takeaway

Being named is not the same as being named correctly.

### What to do

Check that AI answers that name you have the right city, services and details, and fix the sources AI reads when they do not.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry keeps a sourced, dated record of each business, which gives AI a verified source for the business’s name, location and services.

## How should a business measure how often AI recommends it?

Count across many answers under fixed conditions. A business named in 40% of answers has a 95% range of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100.

If visibility is a frequency to be estimated, its measurement belongs to the tradition of the algorithm audit, which studies a system that cannot be inspected directly by querying it repeatedly and recording what it returns.[14](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html#ref-14) Read together, the evidence above suggests five principles for applying that method to local recommendations.

### Five principles for measuring AI visibility

1. **Report a rate, with its conditions.** The core quantity is the share of answers that name a business under a stated set of systems, configurations, locations, phrasings and dates. A rate reported without its conditions cannot be compared with another.
2. **Collect enough answers to support the claim.** One answer records only whether a business was named on that occasion; it cannot distinguish a business named in nine answers out of ten from one named in one out of ten. Under fixed conditions, a business observed in 40% of answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after ten answers and 31% to 50% after one hundred.
3. **Separate inclusion from order.** Whether a business is named and where it appears when named respond to different factors and should be reported separately.
4. **Verify what is counted.** A mention should count only when the business exists, operates in the location asked about and offers the service requested.
5. **Distinguish noise from change.** A shift between two periods is meaningful only when it exceeds the variation seen within a period under the same protocol, the test the Bali census applied.

**Figure 3. A business named in 40% of AI answers has a 95% range of 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100.** Illustrative calculation by Local AI Registry (95% Wilson score intervals, assuming independent answers under fixed conditions), not study data. The range narrows only as answers accumulate. AEO takeaway

Measure a rate, not a rank.

### What to do

Track the share of answers that name your business, collect enough answers to trust it, and treat a change as real only when it is bigger than the normal variation between checks.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s free AI Score gives a broader diagnostic of how findable and recommendable a business is to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity. It is a diagnostic, not the recommendation-frequency measure described in this brief.

## What does this mean for local businesses?

The evidence changes the question worth asking. Whether a given assistant recommends a given business has no stable answer. How often the business is named, by which systems, for which requests, in which places, and how that frequency is moving does. Seen this way, AI visibility is not unknowable. It is measurable in the way other probabilistic systems are measured: through repeated, documented observation, with uncertainty stated and causes claimed only where the evidence supports them.

For local businesses, and for healthcare providers in particular, that discipline separates a reaction to one answer from an understanding of a market position that AI assistants increasingly help to shape. No intervention studied to date guarantees a recommendation. The research does support a narrower and more useful conclusion: visibility in AI-generated local recommendations can be observed, compared and tracked, provided it is estimated from many observations and not inferred from a single answer.

- **Free business record.** A public, owner-claimable record of what AI says about the business, with every fact confirmed by the owner.
- **AI visibility audit.** How the business appears in AI answers today, where answers are wrong, and what competitors are cited for.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does ChatGPT recommend the same businesses every time?

No. AI assistants compose a new answer for every request. When ChatGPT was asked the same local question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both, according to 8ight.AI data reviewed by Local AI Registry. In a census of Bali venues, repeated runs of the same query overlapped by 0.22 for Claude and 0.45 for Gemini.

### How do I know if AI recommends my business?

Ask the same customer questions many times, under the same conditions, and count the share of answers that name your business. One answer only shows whether you were named that one time. Local AI Registry’s free business record and AI visibility audit show what ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity say about a business today.

### How many AI answers do I need to measure my AI visibility?

More than one, and usually many. Local AI Registry calculated that a business named in 40% of answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100 answers, assuming the conditions stay the same.

### Why does AI recommend different businesses in different places?

Place changes the answer. Without web search, the share of real doctors an AI model named fell from 16.3% in the largest third of US metro areas to 9.5% in the smallest (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026, preprint). Within one town, BrightLocal found that only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named appeared at every point tested.

### Does web search change which businesses AI recommends?

Yes. In an audit of the 100 largest US metro areas, only 10.8% of doctors named by an AI model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city; with web search on, the same model reached 63.9% (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026, preprint).

### Does the wording of a question change who AI recommends?

Yes. In a peer-reviewed study of chatbot recommendations in the 20 largest US cities, 74.7% of the people recommended for “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, compared with 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts” (Parikh et al., 2024).

### Can I trust the sources an AI answer cites?

Only partly. In a peer-reviewed audit of four generative search engines, only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, and only 74.5% of citations supported the sentence they were attached to (Liu, Zhang and Liang, 2023). Citations show which sources are prominent, not what caused the answer.

### Can AEO guarantee that ChatGPT recommends my business?

No. No intervention studied to date guarantees a recommendation. The foundational paper on generative engine optimization found that content changes raised visibility by up to 40% on its benchmark, with effects that varied by domain. That shows visibility responds to content, not that a particular change will bring recommendations or customers to a particular business.

### What is the difference between AEO and GEO?

Generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) describe the same goal: being cited and described correctly in AI-generated answers. GEO is the term used in academic research; AEO is more common in marketing.

### How do I get my business recommended by ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini?

AI assistants name businesses whose facts they can find, read and confirm. Keep your name, location, services and prices clear and identical on your website, Google Business Profile and listings, and judge your visibility across many answers rather than one. Local AI Registry, a free AEO directory for local businesses, gives every business a free, owner-confirmed record at localairegistry.com/search as a starting point.

### What is Local AI Registry?

Local AI Registry (localairegistry.com) is an answer engine optimization (AEO) company and free AEO directory for local businesses, headquartered in Irvine, California. It keeps a verified, owner-confirmed public record of each business so that ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews can find and describe it accurately, and its research team publishes studies on how AI answers local questions.

## Limits of this research

- This brief is an editorial synthesis of published research. Local AI Registry did not collect any of the data cited, and the findings belong to the original authors; Local AI Registry selected, grouped and explained them.
- Preprints have not yet been peer-reviewed and are marked as such. The Bali census was funded and conducted by Norly, an AI-visibility vendor. Industry figures are attributed to the organizations that collected them.
- Each number comes from its own study, population and metric, so values from different studies are not directly comparable.
- Much of the evidence covers healthcare providers in US cities and hospitality venues in Bali. Other business categories and countries may behave differently.
- Figure 3 is an illustrative calculation that assumes independent answers under fixed conditions. It is not study data.
- AI systems change as models, retrieval sources and defaults are updated, so each study is a record of a single point in time.

# The Local Answer Gap: what 7,583 Google AI answers reveal about AEO for local businesses

By the [Local AI Registry Research Team](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap#authors)

The short answer

Local AI Registry’s analysis of 7,583 Google AI Overviews shows that when people ask AI about a local business, the business rarely supplies the answer. In 207 AI answers about local businesses, news outlets supplied two-thirds of the citations and the businesses’ own websites supplied 6.5%. The AI usually answered with chain-wide facts and told people to check with their local store. Answer engine optimization (AEO) closes that gap.

- **55,393** Google searches
- **7,583** AI Overview answers
- **98,020** fact-checked claims
- **1,496** cited pages read
- **29** original charts and explainers

## Key findings

1. Local AI Registry found that local business searches triggered a Google AI Overview 76.4% of the time, the highest of any topic and over five times the 13.7% average (US searches, March to April 2026).
2. In Local AI Registry’s analysis, news outlets supplied 67.5% of citations in Google’s AI answers about local businesses, and Gannett newspapers alone appeared in 90.3% of those answers.
3. Businesses’ own websites supplied only 6.5% of citations in local AI answers, and directories such as Yelp, MapQuest and OpenTable supplied 0.5%, according to Local AI Registry.
4. Local AI Registry found that brand websites ranked on Google’s first page in 147 of 157 brand questions but were cited by Google’s AI in only 70.
5. 83.6% of local AI answers told people to check with their local store, and only 1 of 207 gave a street address or phone number, Local AI Registry found.
6. When Google’s AI attributed a local fact to a store locator, app or official site, 51.6% of those claims were not supported by any page it cited, according to Local AI Registry.
7. Cited social media posts had a median of 8 readable words, and 78% were too thin for AI to verify anything, in Local AI Registry’s review of 1,496 cited pages.
8. Asking the same local question in different words changed about two-thirds of the sources Google’s AI cited, Local AI Registry found.
9. Only 2 of 39,676 queries in public AI search research datasets ask an AI to find a local service provider, according to Local AI Registry’s census.

## What is AEO, and how is it different from SEO?

Search engine optimization (SEO) gets a business into a list of blue links. Answer engine optimization (AEO), also called generative engine optimization (GEO), gets a business into the answer itself: the paragraph that Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity or Microsoft Copilot writes before anyone clicks. To write that paragraph, the AI pieces together facts from sources across the internet. If it can’t find clear, consistent facts about a business, it guesses, hedges or leaves the business out.

Local AI Registry is a local AEO company. It builds a verified public record for each local business, has the owner confirm it, and pushes those facts to the places AI reads. This study asks a simple question: when AI answers a local question today, where do its facts come from, and what should a local business do about it?

![Illustration comparing a search results page of blue links (SEO) with an AI answer box that cites a few sources (AEO)](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration.png)

**Illustration 1. SEO gets you into the list. AEO gets you into the answer.** Search engine optimization (SEO) earns a place in a list of links. Answer engine optimization (AEO) earns a place inside the AI-written answer that appears before any links. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/seo-vs-aeo-explained-illustration.png)

Answer engine optimization (AEO)
:   Making a business’s facts clear, consistent and machine-readable so AI systems include it accurately in their answers.

Generative engine optimization (GEO)
:   The academic term for optimizing content to be cited by generative AI search engines; used interchangeably with AEO.

Google AI Overview
:   The AI-written answer Google shows above search results for many queries, with links to the sources it cited.

Citation
:   A source link the AI attaches to its answer. Being cited is how a business’s own pages shape what AI says.

Local intent
:   A search about a physical place: hours, location, services, availability, or finding a provider nearby.

AI visibility
:   How often, how prominently and how accurately a business is named in AI answers, measured as a rate across many answers to the same question.

Google Business Profile
:   Google’s free business listing, which holds a location’s hours, address, services and reviews, and which Google’s AI appears to draw on for store-level facts.

LocalBusiness structured data
:   Schema.org markup on a website that states a business’s name, address, hours and services in a format machines read directly.

## Is anyone studying how AI answers local questions?

Almost no one. Across 39,676 unique queries in four public AI-search research datasets, 239 concern a physical business and only 2 ask an AI to find a local service provider.

![Table of four public AI search datasets: 39,676 unique queries, 239 about physical businesses, 2 asking for a local provider](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/public-ai-search-datasets-local-query-census.png)

**Figure 1. Only 2 of 39,676 public AI-search research queries ask AI to find a local provider.** Across four public AI-search datasets, 239 of 39,676 unique queries (0.6%) concern a physical business, and only 2 ask an AI to find a local service provider. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/public-ai-search-datasets-local-query-census.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/public-ai-search-datasets-local-query-census.png)

| Dataset | Unique queries | About a physical business | Ask for a local provider |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Organikpi, 13 public datasets | 7,045 | 2 | 2 |
| Cited.io, Oct 2026 | 23 | 0 | 0 |
| Total | 39,676 | 239 | 2 |

Every public dataset we found studies informational, software or news queries. The only local questions with real AI answers attached are national chains’ holiday hours, so that is where we looked. It is a clean test: a simple, verifiable fact about a physical place. It also means most AEO advice for local businesses rests on very little local evidence.

## How we did this research

We re-analyzed the raw records released with Measuring Google AI Overviews: Activation, Source Quality, Claim Fidelity, and Publisher Impact (Xu, Iqbal and Montgomery, IMC 2026). The dataset covers 55,393 trending Google searches in the United States from March 13 to April 21, 2026, including 7,583 AI Overviews, every cited link, the page-one results shown beside each answer, the saved text of cited pages, and fact-check verdicts for 98,020 claims.

- **Local filter.** We tagged searches about a physical business’s hours, open status, closures or “near me,” then read every match by hand. That produced 271 local searches, 207 AI answers and 189 unique questions.
- **Comparison group.** The other 7,376 AI answers in the dataset.
- **Source groups.** Every cited domain was sorted into owner groups, including Gannett newspapers (31 domains) and TEGNA TV stations (13 domains), using their published lists of owned outlets.
- **Replication check.** Our extraction found the same 7,583 AI Overviews the paper reports, and our overall unsupported-claim rate (11.03%) matches its published 11.0%.

![Bar chart of local business searches by collection day in March and April 2026, peaking at 185 on April 6](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/local-business-searches-by-day-easter-2026.png)

**Figure 2. ## How often does Google’s AI answer local business questions?

More often than any other topic: 76.4% of local business searches showed a Google AI Overview, against 13.7% of all searches.

AEO takeaway

AI trusts what others publish about you more than what you publish yourself.

### What to do

Get your facts into third-party sources AI already reads: local news, press releases and community roundups. Earned coverage is the citation layer for local answers.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Press releases and media distribution put a business’s confirmed facts on news sites, and the Local AI Registry record itself is an independent third-party source AI can cite.

## Does ranking on Google mean AI will use your website?

No. Brand websites ranked on page one in 147 of 157 brand questions, but the AI cited them in only 70.

AEO takeaway

SEO gets you ranked. AEO gets you used.

### What to do

Write pages that answer one question each in plain sentences, such as “Are you open on Easter?” or “What do you charge for Botox?” Put the answer in the first line, then the details.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s AEO content work builds question-and-answer pages, topical maps and structured data on the client’s own site, so the page that ranks is also the page AI can quote.

## Why does Google’s AI tell people to “check with your local store”?

Because it answers local questions with national facts. 83.6% of local answers hedged, and only 1 of 207 named an address.

![Waffle chart of 207 squares, 173 highlighted for answers that hedged with check locally or call ahead](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-answers-telling-people-to-check-local-store-waffle.png)

**Figure 14. 173 of 207 local AI answers told people to check with their local store.** 83.6% of local AI answers sent the reader back to the store (“check your local store,” “call ahead,” “hours may vary”), against 2.6% of other answers. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-answers-telling-people-to-check-local-store-waffle.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-answers-telling-people-to-check-local-store-waffle.png)

**Data behind this chart:**

| Group | Hedged |
| --- | --- |
| Local answers | 83.6% |
| Other answers | 2.6% |

![Grouped bar chart: 83.6% of local answers hedge, 65.7% frame the answer at chain level, 0.5% give an address](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/how-ai-answers-local-questions-national-framing.png)

**Figure 15. AI answers local questions with national facts.** 65.7% of local answers spoke about “all locations” or “most stores” (vs 2.3% of other answers), and 83.6% hedged (vs 2.6%). National facts are the AI’s default for local questions. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/how-ai-answers-local-questions-national-framing.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/how-ai-answers-local-questions-national-framing.png)

| --- | --- | --- |
| Tells you to check locally | 83.6% | 2.6% |
| Answers at chain level | 65.7% | 2.3% |
| Gives address or phone | 0.5% | 0.8% |

![Waffle chart of 207 squares with a single highlighted square for the one answer that gave an address or phone number](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-local-answers-with-address-or-phone-waffle.png)

**Figure 16. 1 of 207 local AI answers named a street address or phone number.** Only 1 of 207 local AI answers gave a street address or phone number. The AI answered about chains, not places. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-local-answers-with-address-or-phone-waffle.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-local-answers-with-address-or-phone-waffle.png)

| --- | --- |
| 207 | 1 |

The AI knows its answer is not about your location, so it hands the question back to the reader. Whoever publishes location-level facts in a form AI can read gets to answer instead of a hedge.

AEO takeaway

Location-level facts are the gap. Fill it and you replace the hedge.

### What to do

Publish your own hours, holiday hours, address, services and prices for your exact location, in plain text and in LocalBusiness structured data, and keep your Google Business Profile current.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Owners claim their Local AI Registry record for free and confirm each fact. Local AI Registry manages the Google Business Profile, adds LocalBusiness structured data that links back to the verified record, and keeps holiday hours current.

## Can Google’s AI actually read your website?

Often not. When the AI said “the store locator says,” 51.6% of those claims were not supported by any page it cited.

![Bar chart: 51.6% of local claims quoting a store locator or app were unsupported, vs 6.7% of other local claims](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-store-locator-claims-unsupported-rate.png)

**Figure 17. When Google’s AI says “the store locator says,” half the time it can’t show it.** 16 of 31 local claims that cited a store locator, app or official site (51.6%) were not supported by any page the AI cited, against 6.7% of other local claims. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-store-locator-claims-unsupported-rate.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-store-locator-claims-unsupported-rate.png)

**Data behind this chart:**

| Claim type | Unsupported | Total | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local claims quoting a store locator, app or official site | 16 | 31 | 51.6% |
| All other local claims | 148 | 2,222 | 6.7% |
| Non-local claims quoting an official source | 49 | 465 | 10.5% |

Examples written by the AI and not found in its sources include “The Aldi store locator indicates Easter Sunday: Closed” and “Target Store Locator lists Easter Sunday as closed.” The pattern suggests the AI gets store-level hours from somewhere it does not cite, likely Google’s own business listing data, and attributes them to a locator page it could not read.

![Illustration of three page types: a news article full of readable text, a store locator page made mostly of scripts, and a social post with a photo and a few words](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration.png)

**Illustration 4. What Google’s AI can actually read on a page.** News pages the AI cited had about 500 readable words. Store locator pages were mostly scripts, and the median cited social post had 8 readable words. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration.png)

![Two by two of source types by how often they were cited and how often their pages had readable text; social is cited but 78% unreadable](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2.png)

**Figure 18. Cited vs readable: what Google’s AI could actually read.** News pages were both cited and readable. Social posts were cited in 48% of local answers but 78% were thin (median 8 words). 11% of businesses’ own pages were thin. [SVG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2.svg) · [PNG](https://localairegistry.com/research/local-answer-gap/images/cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2.png)

| AOL, Yahoo, MSN | 43.0% | 123 | 639 | 0.0% |

| Everything else | 39.1% | 113 | 569 | 1.8% |

**Figure 19. Social posts the AI cited had a median of 8 readable words.** The median cited social post had 8 readable words. Store locator pages were also thin: Trader Joe’s store search had 97 words and Cracker Barrel’s Easter page 18. AEO takeaway

If AI can’t read it, it can’t cite it, and it may misquote it.

### What to do

Keep key facts in plain HTML text, not inside store-locator scripts, images or social posts. A one-page “hours and holidays” page beats a widget. Post updates on your website as well as on Instagram or Facebook.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s technical AEO work makes sites readable to AI crawlers: text versions of key facts, schema markup, an llms.txt file, and readable descriptions on photos and media.

## Do AI answers about local businesses stay the same?

The verdict does; the sources don’t. Different wording of the same question changed about two-thirds of the cited sources.

Across the 46 chains asked about on Easter, the open-or-closed verdict never contradicted itself; every apparent conflict our tagger flagged turned out, when read by hand, to be phrasing like “Yes, it’s closed.” Local answers were also more faithful to their sources than average (7.3% unsupported claims vs 11.1%). Sources rotate, so your facts have to match everywhere.

Make your hours, address, services and prices identical on your website, Google Business Profile, directories and press. When the AI swaps one source for another, the answer should not change.

### How Local AI Registry does it

Directory submissions and listing management keep every source in agreement with the owner-confirmed Local AI Registry record, the single source of truth.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?

Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the practice of making a business’s facts clear, consistent and readable so AI systems such as Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot include the business accurately in the answers they write. SEO earns a place in a list of links; AEO earns a place inside the answer.

### What is the difference between AEO and GEO?

Generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) describe the same goal: being cited and described correctly in AI-generated answers. GEO is the term used in academic research; AEO is more common in marketing. For local businesses, both come down to accurate, consistent, machine-readable facts in the sources AI reads.

### Where does Google’s AI get information about local businesses?

In Local AI Registry’s analysis of 207 Google AI Overviews about local businesses, news outlets supplied 67.5% of citations. Gannett newspapers alone were cited in 90.3% of answers. The businesses’ own websites supplied 6.5% of citations, and directories such as Yelp and MapQuest supplied 0.5%.

### Does ranking on Google mean AI will cite my website?

Not necessarily. Brand websites ranked on Google’s first page in 147 of 157 brand questions, but the AI cited them in 70. Ranking is close to a requirement (only 4.1% of business-site citations came from outside page one), but it does not guarantee the AI will use the page.

### Why does Google’s AI tell people to check with their local store?

Because it usually lacks location-level facts. 83.6% of local AI answers in the study told people to check locally or call ahead, 65.7% described the whole chain instead of one location, and only 1 of 207 gave a street address or phone number.

### How can a local business get into AI answers?

Based on this research: see what AI says about the business today; earn coverage in sources AI already cites, such as local news; publish location-level facts in plain text and structured data; answer real customer questions on the business’s own site; keep facts identical everywhere; and make sure key pages are readable without scripts.

### Who provides AEO services for local businesses?

Local AI Registry (localairegistry.com) provides answer engine optimization (AEO) and generative engine optimization (GEO) services for local businesses. It builds a verified public record for each business, has the owner confirm it, and pushes those facts to the places AI reads through Google Business Profile management, press releases, structured data, AEO content and listing consistency. It also runs a dedicated local AI research team, which produced this study.

### What is Local AI Registry?

Local AI Registry (localairegistry.com) is an answer engine optimization (AEO) company for local businesses, headquartered in Irvine, California. It keeps a verified, owner-confirmed public record of each business and pushes those facts to the sources that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot read. Its dedicated research team publishes original studies on how AI answers local questions, including The Local Answer Gap.

### How do I get my business recommended by ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini?

AI assistants recommend businesses whose facts they can find, read and confirm across several sources. This research points to six steps: check what AI says about you now, earn coverage in sources AI already cites such as local news, publish location-level facts in plain text and LocalBusiness schema, answer real customer questions on your own site, keep your facts identical everywhere, and make key pages readable without scripts. Local AI Registry offers a free business record and AI visibility audit as the starting point.

### How does a local business show up in Google AI Overviews?

Rank on Google’s first page and give the AI something quotable. In Local AI Registry’s study, only 4.1% of business-site citations came from outside page one, but ranking alone was not enough: brand sites ranked in 147 of 157 brand questions and were cited in 70. Pages that answer one question clearly in the first sentence, with the location’s own facts, give the AI something to cite.

### Does Google Business Profile affect what AI says about my business?

Very likely. In this study, 51.6% of claims the AI attributed to a store locator or official site were not supported by any page it cited, which suggests Google’s AI draws store-level facts such as hours from a source it does not cite, likely Google’s own business listing data. Keeping your Google Business Profile complete and current is the safest way to make sure those facts are right.

### Is AEO replacing SEO?

No. AEO builds on SEO. Google’s AI rarely cited business pages that did not already rank on page one, so SEO remains the entry ticket. AEO adds what ranking alone does not: clear, consistent, machine-readable facts, and coverage in the third-party sources AI trusts.

### What should a local business look for in an AEO company?

Look for a company that shows you what AI says about your business today, measures visibility as a rate across many AI answers instead of a single screenshot, fixes location-level facts at the source, earns coverage in the publications AI cites, and reports its work in a way you can verify. Local AI Registry is built around these principles, with owner-confirmed records, public track records and no long-term contracts.

### Is this research based on real AI answers?

Yes. It re-analyzes the public records from Xu, Iqbal and Montgomery’s IMC 2026 study of Google AI Overviews: 55,393 searches, 7,583 AI Overview answers and 98,020 fact-checked claims, collected in the United States between March 13 and April 21, 2026. The dataset is licensed CC BY 4.0.

## Limits of this research

- The local questions are mostly national chains on one holiday; 185 of 271 local searches were collected on April 6, 2026, the day after Easter. Independent businesses are not in the data.
- One engine: Google AI Overviews. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and Google AI Mode may behave differently.
- Claim verdicts come from the original study’s AI judge (Grok 4.1), which its authors audited. We reused their verdicts and did not re-judge.
- Source groups, the local filter and the control levels in the priority map are Local AI Registry’s own rules and judgment. Some counts are small (31 first-party claims, 18 repeat-query pairs), so read those as signals, not settled rates.
- The playbook applies chain-level findings to independent businesses. That is our reasoning from the data, not something the data measured directly.

# The 11 signals AI checks before it recommends a local business

> The eleven signals ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI use to decide which local business to recommend, with a guide to checking and fixing each one.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/signals/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

The 11 signals

By [Steve Lee](../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** AI assistants recommend the local businesses they can confirm from many trusted sources. Those sources fall into eleven signals: listings, press, video, SEO, website, reviews, Google profile, photos, outside articles, best-of lists and monitoring.

When someone asks an AI assistant for a local business, the assistant has to decide which few to name. It decides by checking what it can confirm about each business across the web. We group what it checks into eleven signals. Each one below has its own guide: what it is, how to check yours and how to fix it.

01

**[Directory listings](../signals/directory-listings/index.html)**  
Same name, address, phone and hours everywhere. AI assistants compare what different websites say about your business.

02

**[Press coverage](../signals/pr/index.html)**  
Real news coverage AI can cite. Yes.

03

**[Video](../signals/video/index.html)**  
Explainer videos that answer what customers ask. Video helps in two ways.

04

**[SEO](../signals/seo/index.html)**  
The Google searches you rank for, and should. Yes.

05

**[Website](../signals/web-management/index.html)**  
A fast site with the code AI reads. Your site needs to load fast, work on a phone, state plainly what you do and where, and include structured data (schema) that labels your business, services, hours and reviews in a format machines read without guessing.

06

**[Reviews](../signals/reputation/index.html)**  
Reviews, ratings and replies across sites. Reviews are one of the main things assistants use to decide who to recommend.

07

**[Google profile](../signals/google-profile/index.html)**  
Complete, active and posting every week. Yes, heavily for Google's own AI answers and Gemini, which draw on Google's local data, and indirectly for other assistants that read Google results.

08

**[Photos](../signals/photo-codifying/index.html)**  
Photos labeled so AI can read what they show. Partly.

09

**[Outside articles](../signals/third-party-articles/index.html)**  
Features about you on independent sites. Assistants trust what independent sites say about you more than what you say about yourself.

10

**[Best-of guides](../signals/best-of-guides/index.html)**  
A place on the local best-of lists AI quotes. Often, yes.

11

**[AI monitoring](../signals/ai-monitoring/index.html)**  
What every assistant says about you, each month. Ask it, regularly and the same way each time.

## How the signals add up

No single signal decides the answer. Assistants look for agreement: the same facts in many places, and outside sources that back up what you say about yourself. That's why the [AI Score](../glossary/index.html#ai-score) looks at all eleven together, and why our [methodology](../methodology/index.html) weighs them as a set. Start with the [complete guide](../guide/index.html) or see the signals that matter most [for your industry](../for/ai/index.html).

From our data · 3D

New data from our research team

**73%**

73% of the 128,400+ local businesses Local AI Registry has scored are named by zero AI assistants (our estimate from AI-visibility checks). [Local AI Registry data](../methodology/index.html)

**1 in 75**

Across the businesses we've scored, nearly two in three land below 45 out of 100 on the AI Score, and barely one in seventy-five clears 65. [What is an AI Score?](../journal/what-is-an-ai-score/index.html)

**85.6%**

In a census of every venue in two markets, 85.6% were never recommended by any of four assistants. Being named was associated with having a website, more reviews, listed prices and web mentions (Pitenin 2026, preprint, reviewed in our brief). [How Often AI Recommends Your Business, LAIR-R-2026-002](../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html)

# How do I know what AI says about my business?

> Ask it, regularly and the same way each time. Run the questions your customers ask across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google's AI answers, Perplexity and others every.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/signals/ai-monitoring/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

What we handle · 11 of 11

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** Ask it, regularly and the same way each time. Run the questions your customers ask across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google's AI answers, Perplexity and others every month, and record whether you're named, how you're described and which sources each assistant cites.

## Why monitoring matters

AI answers change. Assistants update their models, change their sources and refresh their data. A business that was recommended last month can disappear without warning. Monitoring is how you notice, and the sources each assistant cites tell you exactly where to work next.

New data from our research team

**two-thirds**

Rewording the same local question changed about two-thirds of the sources Google's AI cited. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

**29%**

When ChatGPT got the same local question about 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses it named appeared in both answers (8ight.AI, reviewed in our brief). [How Often AI Recommends Your Business, LAIR-R-2026-002](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html)

**0.46**

Asked the same query twice, Google Search shared 0.78 of its sources, AI Overviews 0.66 and Gemini 0.46 (Grossman et al., SIGIR 2026, reviewed in our brief). [How Often AI Recommends Your Business, LAIR-R-2026-002](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html)

## What does the research say?

From [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html), our study of how Google's AI answers local business questions, and [AI Answer Watch](../../answer-watch/index.html), our screenshots of ChatGPT's answers. Every number links to its chart.

## What we do for you

A question is a category, not a phrase. You pick the searches you want to win, and we write a set of questions around each one: what it costs, whether it is worth doing, who does it near the town, how to choose a provider.

ChatGPT and Perplexity are asked in a real browser and we keep a screenshot. Gemini is checked directly, so we keep its words but no picture.

### How it runs

3. **The assistants are asked** ChatGPT and Perplexity in a browser with a screenshot, Gemini checked directly. A question is asked once per calendar month, so nothing is bought twice.
4. **The answer is read and stored** We record the answer text, the businesses named in it, and where you came in. If a check fails, we record it as a failed check, never as you not being named.

**Why it moves the AI answer** Capture is the measurement, not the work. It tells you which questions you already win, and it is the only honest way to know whether the rest of the work moved anything.

# Why do directory listings matter for AI recommendations?

> AI assistants compare what different websites say about your business.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/signals/directory-listings/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

What we handle · 01 of 11

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** AI assistants compare what different websites say about your business. When your name, address, phone number and hours match on every directory, the assistant can be confident it has the right business. When they conflict, it hedges or names someone else.

## What AI is checking

Before an assistant recommends a local business, it has to be sure the business is real, open and where it says it is. It checks that by reading many sources at once: maps apps, review sites, industry directories, data aggregators and your own website. Each one is a vote. Matching votes build confidence; mismatched votes create doubt.

The most common mismatches are small: an old suite number, a former phone number, holiday hours that never got changed back, or a business name written three different ways.

New data from our research team

**88%**

45% of consumers now use AI for local discovery, up from 6%, and 88% fact-check the result (BrightLocal Local Consumer Review Survey 2026, cited in The Convergence). [The Convergence](../../proof/the-convergence-white-paper/index.html)

**83.6%**

83.6% of local AI answers told people to check with their local store, and only 1 of 207 gave a street address or phone number. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

**3.5%**

Only 3.5% of businesses ChatGPT named in localized searches appeared at every test point across a town (BrightLocal, reviewed in our brief). [How Often AI Recommends Your Business, LAIR-R-2026-002](../../research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-business/index.html)

## What does the research say?

From [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html), our study of how Google's AI answers local business questions. Every number links to its chart.

[**~35%** of cited sources stayed the same when the same question was worded differently](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#ai-answer-source-overlap-by-wording)[**83.6%** of local AI answers told people to check with their local store](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#ai-answers-telling-people-to-check-local-store-waffle)[**1 of 207** local AI answers gave a street address or phone number](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#ai-local-answers-with-address-or-phone-waffle)

**One confirmed record, pushed everywhere AI looks.** Because AI rotates between sources, a business’s facts need to match on its website, Google Business Profile, directories and press. Local AI Registry starts from one owner-confirmed record.Illustration 6, [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration.svg) · [PNG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/single-source-of-truth-for-ai-local-aeo-illustration.png)

**Ask the same thing in different words and two-thirds of the sources change.** “Is Target open on Easter” and “Target Easter hours,” asked the same day, shared about 35% of cited sources on average. The verdict stayed the same; the sources rotated.Figure 20, [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#ai-answer-source-overlap-by-wording), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-answer-source-overlap-by-wording.svg) · [PNG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/ai-answer-source-overlap-by-wording.png)

## What we do for you

We check which directories already carry your business, then order listings on the ones that do not.

Twenty three general hosts for everyone: Yelp, Apple Maps, Facebook, the BBB, Yellow Pages, Foursquare, Nextdoor, Trustpilot and the rest. Your trade adds its own on top, which takes a medical practice to forty: Zocdoc, Healthgrades, WebMD, RealSelf, Vitals and eleven more.

A reading says what we found. A directory we could not find you on is recorded as not found, which is a different fact from not present, and we say which one it is.

Readings age out after thirty days, so a page you look at today is a recent read rather than a number from when you signed up.

### What you get

- A page listing each directory and where you stand on it.
- A submission order covering only the ones you are missing.
- One record pushed out, so the phone number is the same everywhere it is printed.
- A re-check whenever you or your expert asks for one, and readings retired at thirty days rather than shown stale.

### How it runs

1. **You confirm the two fields that print** Phone and address. A directory submission prints both and a wrong one is slow and expensive to take back, so nothing is ordered until you have confirmed them.
2. **The presence audit runs** Every host on your roster is checked, so the order covers only what is genuinely missing.
3. **The order is queued** Queued, never auto-confirmed. A person on our team confirms every purchase, under a spending limit, so nothing buys itself.
4. **Progress shows on your page** Premium lists each directory once it is live, under Directory submissions. There is no email for this, because a queue is not news.

**Why it moves the AI answer** An assistant does not read one source. It reads many, and a business whose address disagrees across them is a business it has reason to leave out.

## How to check yours

1. Search your business name plus your city in Google, Bing and Apple Maps.
2. Open the first two pages of results and write down the name, address, phone and hours each one shows.
3. Mark every line that differs from your own website.
4. Ask ChatGPT and Gemini for your phone number and hours. If they get it wrong, a directory is feeding them the wrong data.

# Does my Google Business Profile affect AI recommendations?

**Short answer** Yes, heavily for Google's own AI answers and Gemini, which draw on Google's local data, and indirectly for other assistants that read Google results. A complete, accurate and active profile is one of the highest-value fixes for any local business.

## Why it matters beyond Google Maps

Your Google Business Profile is the most widely read record of your business on the internet. [Google's AI answers](../../ai/google-ai-overviews/index.html) and [Gemini](../../ai/gemini/index.html) lean on it directly. Other assistants often see it through search results. When it's thin or out of date, every assistant gets a weaker picture of you.

## What we do for you

We write the posts on your Google Business Profile and send each one to you before it publishes.

A post is drafted from things we hold about you: the services on your listing, the searches you picked, your photos and your brand rules. Nothing is written from a template.

Every draft is checked against our writing standard, then by an automatic check that blocks the usual mistakes: the wrong town, a made-up statistic or a medical claim.

You choose the cadence. Daily, a few times a week, weekly, or paused.

### What you get

- A draft in your approvals queue with the question it is aimed at named on it.
- An email with the draft and the date it publishes if you leave it alone.
- Edit, approve or decline. A declined draft is not published and the next one takes a different angle.
- The published post on your listing, with the date and the text kept on your account.

### How it runs

1. **A slot comes due** Your cadence decides when. A post drafted inside the same window is not drafted again, so a weekly cadence is a post a week and not a post a day.
2. **The draft is written and checked** Written from your own facts, then checked and rewritten up to three times until it passes. A draft that still fails on the third pass never reaches your queue, and the next slot tries a different angle.
3. **You see it first** The draft lands in your queue and an email goes to you with a publish date three business days out. If it sits unread, one reminder follows.
4. **It publishes** On approval, or on the date in its email if you leave it alone. Decline it and it doesn't go up. You can set posts to wait for your yes in your settings.

**Why it moves the AI answer** An assistant answering a local question reads the Google listing, and a listing that has said nothing in four months reads as a business that may not be trading.

## Complete every field

- The right primary category, plus every secondary category that fits.
- Every service, each with a short description.
- Hours, including holiday hours.
- Photos of the outside, inside, team and work, labeled clearly.
- Questions and answers filled in by you.

# Can AI understand the photos of my business?

> Partly. AI can now describe images, but it reads the text around a photo more reliably: the file name, alt text, caption and the page it sits on.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/signals/photo-codifying/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

What we handle · 08 of 11

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** Partly. AI can now describe images, but it reads the text around a photo more reliably: the file name, alt text, caption and the page it sits on. Labeling photos clearly turns them from decoration into evidence of what you do.

## Why labels matter

A photo named IMG\_4821.jpg tells a machine nothing. The same photo named and described as "dental implant consultation room, Irvine" tells it what the room is for and where it is. Multiply that across every photo on your site and profile, and AI gets a much clearer picture of your services and space.

New data from our research team

**78%**

Cited social posts had a median of 8 readable words, and 78% were too thin to verify anything. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

## What does the research say?

From [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html), our study of how Google's AI answers local business questions. Every number links to its chart.

[**8 words** readable on the median social post Google's AI cited](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#readable-words-on-ai-cited-pages-by-source)[**51.6%** of claims citing a store locator or official site had no supporting page](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#ai-store-locator-claims-unsupported-rate)

**What Google’s AI can actually read on a page.** News pages the AI cited had about 500 readable words. Store locator pages were mostly scripts, and the median cited social post had 8 readable words.Illustration 4, [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration.svg) · [PNG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/what-ai-can-read-on-a-web-page-illustration.png)

**Cited vs readable: what Google’s AI could actually read.** News pages were both cited and readable. Social posts were cited in 48% of local answers but 78% were thin (median 8 words). 11% of businesses’ own pages were thin.Figure 18, [The Local Answer Gap](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html#cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2), Local AI Registry Research, 2026 · [SVG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2.svg) · [PNG](../../research/local-answer-gap/images/cited-vs-readable-ai-sources-2x2.png)

## What we do for you

We collect your photos, write the words that travel with each one, and publish them onto your Google listing a few at a time.

Pictures come from three places: your Google listing, your website, and any social profile we hold a link to. Only public pages, and a private one is stepped past.

Two sets of words are written per photo. One is embedded in the file itself, in the fields Google and every modern library read. The other is the description published under the picture on your listing.

Both use only the words on your own service list and what kind of picture it is. We never let AI write a description of a medical image, and before and after photos are never described at all.

### What you get

- A library with every picture we hold on you, for a person to confirm before anything reaches Google.
- Files carrying your business, your service and your location in their own metadata.
- Photos published onto the listing on a slow cadence, one a day, so a backlog drains over a week rather than in a minute.
- A date per photo you can set yourself.

### How it runs

1. **Photos are collected** From the listing, the website and your social links, once per business. You can upload more at any time.
2. **Each one is classified** Against the services on your own record, so the words we attach are a service you actually offer.
3. **The words are written in** Each file gets a title, description, keywords, your city and a credit. We don't describe what's in the picture.
4. **They publish on a drip** One a day per business. Google limits how fast new photos can go up, and a pile posted in one day looks like spam.

**Why it moves the AI answer** A photo with no words attached is invisible to anything reading rather than looking, and the description under it is the part a retrieval system can quote.

## How to codify a photo

1. Rename the file with plain words for what it shows.
2. Write alt text in one sentence: what is in the picture and why it matters.
3. Add a caption on the page where it helps the reader.
4. Place the photo on the page about that service, not in a generic gallery.

# Does press coverage help a local business get recommended by AI?

> Yes. AI assistants trust independent sources more than a business's own website.

Source: https://localairegistry.com/signals/pr/
Updated: 2026-11-15
Publisher: Local AI Registry (https://localairegistry.com)

What we handle · 02 of 11

By [Steve Lee](../../team/steve-lee/index.html), founder of Local AI Registry · Updated November 15, 2026

**Short answer** Yes. AI assistants trust independent sources more than a business's own website. A real news story or feature that names your business is one of the strongest signals that you are established and worth recommending.

## Why AI weighs the press

Your website will always say you are great. An assistant knows that, so it looks for someone else saying it. Local news, trade publications and respected industry sites act as outside proof. When an assistant searches the web to answer a question, those pages are often among the sources it reads.

New data from our research team

**0.737**

In a 75,000-brand study, the top correlate of AI visibility was YouTube and branded web mentions (0.737), not links or pages (Ahrefs, cited in our white paper The Convergence). [The Convergence](../../proof/the-convergence-white-paper/index.html)

**67.5%**

News outlets supplied 67.5% of the citations in Google's AI answers about local businesses. [The Local Answer Gap, LAIR-R-2026-001](../../research/local-answer-gap/index.html)

## What does the research say?

## What we do for you

You choose what the news is, we draft the release, and nothing goes to the wire until you have signed it off.

The topic is yours. A release is irreversible once a wire has it, so we never pick the subject and we never send one without your approval.

The draft is held to the strictest reading of our writing standard. No outcome claim, no credential we do not hold on file, no statistic nobody measured.

Each publication that picks it up is recorded against your account with its address, so the coverage is a list of links rather than a number.

### What you get

- A drafted release on a topic you picked, in your voice.
- A named reminder while it waits, because nothing sends this one for you.
- The publications that carried it, each with the article address.
- The same list printed in your monthly report.

### How it runs

1. **You pick the topic** From your own news. An opening, a new service, a hire, a piece of equipment.
2. **We draft it** The news is the first sentence. The draft carries only facts we hold on you or facts you supplied for this release.
3. **You sign it off** A press release never goes out unless you approve it. If the deadline passes without you sending it, we cancel the order, tell you we did not buy it, and draft a fresh one on the next round.
4. **Coverage is recorded** Every pickup is stored with its publication and its address. If a distributor quotes a reach number, we show it as their number, never as something we measured.

**Why it moves the AI answer** A mention on a publication you do not own is the one kind of evidence about you that you did not write, which is why an assistant weighs it differently from your own site.

## What counts

- Local news stories, features and expert quotes.
- Trade and industry publications.
- Interviews and podcasts with show notes that name you.
- Award lists from real organizations.

Paid press releases that only appear on syndication networks count for much less. They are easy to buy, so they prove little.
